items.title: U.S. stocks climb amid shaky trading in markets worldwide
items.description: U.S. stocks are climbing amid shaky trading for financial markets worldwide, as AI stocks keep swinging and Brazilian stocks tumble.

items._ogDesc: U.S. stocks are climbing amid shaky trading for financial markets worldwide, as AI stocks keep swinging and Brazilian stocks tumble.
items.body:
NEW YORK — U.S. stocks are climbing Monday amid shaky trading for financial markets worldwide, as AI stocks keep swinging and Brazilian stocks tumble.

The S&P 500 rose 0.8 per cent and more than recovered its losses from last week, pulling within 1.6 per cent of its all-time high set earlier this month. The Dow Jones Industrial Average was up 154 points, or 0.3 per cent, as of 1:15 p.m. Eastern time, and the Nasdaq composite was 1.1 per cent higher.

The strongest lift for the market came from Nvidia, which rose 2.5 per cent. That helped the chip company recover some of its drop from three straight losing weeks, its longest such streak since June, and maintain its position as the largest stock on Wall Street above Apple.

  • S&P 500 market updates here

But stocks elsewhere in the artificial-intelligence industry remained unsettled. They’ve been swerving on worries about whether their industry’s boom is under threat because of how expensive it’s become for companies to borrow money to build data centers and buy more AI chips.

Meta helps lead the swings

Meta Platforms bounced up and down after outlining plans to raise US$35 billion by selling stock to help pay for its AI investments. It also said it could raise another US$60 billion by selling shares of a new class of its stock once it begins trading. Meta’s stock initially dropped more than 2 per cent, but it quickly flipped to a gain and then pulled back to a loss of 0.2 per cent.

Meta said Nvidia, Advanced Micro Devices and Broadcom have already indicated they may buy a total of US$5 billion of stock in its offering. That’s a signal of strong interest from big chip companies that stand to benefit from additional AI investments. But it also gives fuel to critics of “circular financing” who say it raises the risk if AI isn’t as successful as expected.

Worries remain about borrowing for AI

SpaceX, Elon Musk’s rocket company that also runs the xAI business, had similar swings. It opened with a loss and then flipped to a gain of 0.9 per cent after it agreed to a roughly US$40 billion deal with an entity managed by Apollo Global Management to lease AI computing power.

Musk warned over the weekend that hundreds of companies that rent out AI computing power are under threat because of the difficulty in borrowing money, saying on his social-media platform, X, that they could face “guppy-level death and consolidation.”

  • Latest updates on artificial intelligence news here

CoreWeave, a company that’s borrowed money to buy AI computing power that it rents to customers, has been at the center of investors’ worries in recent weeks. On Monday, it dropped 5.5 per cent quickly after trading began, only to flip to a gain of 5.1 per cent. Such minute-to-minute swings have become commonplace for it in recent days.

It’s a big week for profit reports

Profit reports from huge tech companies this upcoming week could offer more details about how spending on AI is going, and whether it’s producing the profits and productivity that proponents promised.

Alphabet and Microsoft will report their latest quarterly results on Wednesday, with Amazon to follow on Thursday.

Companies across all industries are under pressure to report strong growth in their profits. Expectations for big growth are what allowed their stock prices to run to records recently despite worries about high inflation, high interest rates and other concerns.

Verizon Communications fell 2.8 per cent even though it reported a stronger profit for the summer than analysts expected, as its revenue fell short of forecasts.

Roughly one out of every three stocks in the S&P 500 is scheduled to report its latest quarterly results this week.

Brazilian stocks tumble following mixed moves in other markets

In stock markets abroad, Brazilian stocks fell sharply after President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva won reelection in a result that surprised investors.

The worry among investors is that he could increase the government’s spending and put more pressure on its debt. The Bovespa stock index in Brazil dropped 14.6 per cent.

Other governments around the world are also feeling pressure because of their high debt loads and worries about strained budgets. France has been at the center of the worries recently following violent protests in the country.

  • Latest updates on international news here

But yields on French government bonds eased Monday, and its CAC 40 stock index rose 0.8 per cent for one of the world’s better moves. Indexes also rose in other European markets following a mixed finish in Asia.

The European Central Bank and the Bank of Japan will be meeting to vote on interest rates later this week.

Yields ease ahead of the U.S. Federal Reserve’s meeting

In the U.S. bond market, yields fell for longer-term Treasurys. The yield on the 10-year Treasury fell to 4.98 per cent from 5.00 per cent late Friday and from more than 5.30 per cent earlier this month.

The two-year Treasury yield edged up to 4.71 per cent from 4.69 per cent late Friday. It more closely tracks expectations for what the Federal Reserve will do with overnight interest rates, and the widespread expectation is that it will say on Wednesday that it is leaving the federal funds rate alone following its latest meeting.

The Fed last month hiked the fed funds rate for the first time in three years in hopes of slowing inflation, which has remained much higher than anyone would like.

Oil prices swing

The price for a barrel of Brent crude fell toward US$109 in the morning, but it later erased the losses and returned to US$111.40. It remains near the high end of its range since the war with Iran began. The highest price for the most actively traded contract in the market for Brent crude since then is nearly US$120, reached in March.

Stan Choe, The Associated Press

AP Business Writers Michelle Chapman and Elaine Kurtenbach contributed to this report.

items.title: Bank of Canada now expected to hike key rate as it faces 'pivotal decision'
items.description: Expectations are rising that the Bank of Canada will indeed raise interest rates this week as it considers the effect of higher energy prices on the economy.

items._ogDesc: Expectations are rising that the Bank of Canada will indeed raise interest rates this week as it considers the effect of higher energy prices on the economy.
items.body:
Expectations are rising that the Bank of Canada will indeed raise its benchmark interest rate this week as it considers the effect of higher energy prices on the economy.   

Financial market odds for a rate hike were just over 83 per cent as of Monday afternoon, according to LSEG Data & Analytics. The central bank’s planned interest rate announcement on Wednesday will also include an updated monetary policy report.

The Bank of Canada has held its policy rate at 2.25 per cent for seven consecutive meetings. 

RBC economists said in a note to clients Thursday that they are now expecting a quarter-point hike as the central bank faces a “pivotal decision amid evolving economic conditions.”

  • Latest economic news on BNNBloomberg.ca

Last week, Statistics Canada reported the annual inflation rate rose to 3.1 per cent in September as the war in the Middle East continued to drive up gasoline prices. Excluding gasoline, the consumer price index rose 2.2 per cent year-over-year in September, easing from 2.4 per cent in August, suggesting higher energy prices haven’t significantly spread throughout the economy yet.  

Meanwhile, jobs data from StatCan released earlier this month showed the labour market stalled for a second month in a row in September as the economy lost 68,000 positions. 

However, the RBC economists said they have “very low conviction” on a rate hike happening this week, and see a significant chance the Bank of Canada instead uses the meeting to set up a hike in December or January.

“While we don’t see an immediate need for the BoC to hike now, at the same time, a 25-basis-point increase in the overnight rate on Wednesday won’t materially change our medium-term economic outlook compared to a December or January hike,” the note reads. 

RBC assistant chief economist Nathan Janzen said in an interview that recent comments from Bank of Canada governor Tiff Macklem appeared to drive the change in expectations. 

While speaking from the sidelines of the International Monetary Fund meetings in Bangkok, Macklem warned that persistently high global energy prices will drive up the inflation outlook at home.    

“That essentially just emphasized that the central bank is increasingly worried about the potential impact of higher oil prices on future, broader inflation pressures, and they feel confident enough the economic backdrop is going to gradually continue to improve,” Janzen said.    

The Bank of Canada released its latest business outlook survey last week, which suggested that business sentiment improved on average in the third quarter. However, it found that concerns remained about rising costs and the war in the Middle East. 

“All the economic data that we’ve had to date is consistent with the view that the central bank, the Bank of Canada, was getting closer to raising interest rates,” Janzen said. 

Canadian interest rates are still relatively low, he added, and the neutral range — where rates are neither helping nor hurting the economy — sits between 2.25 per cent and 3.25 per cent.  

TD Bank economist Marc Ercolao said in an interview that it is clear the Bank of Canada is becoming more concerned about the persistence of rising energy prices, “and that’s what’s starting to change the calculus.” 

While a hike is likely, he said there are also arguments for the bank to hold its key rate.  

“There’s interest-sensitive parts of the economy, particularly housing, that are already dealing with higher bond yields and too much additional tightening risks some unnecessary weaker demand in that space,” Ercolao said. 

“Overall, Canada’s economy is growing, but it’s not necessarily overheating by any means.” 

The impact of U.S. trade tensions on overall investment and a weakening labour market also support a decision to hold interest rates, he said. 

He said a hike on Wednesday would be a risk management measure to prevent the inflation shock from becoming more persistent. 

Ercolao said higher energy prices are a double-edged sword for the domestic economy. 

“On one hand, higher energy prices are good for producers and government, and corporate revenue intake. It creates higher incomes especially in commodity-producing provinces,” he said.

  • Latest updates on investing here

“But at the same time, it’s households especially that feel the pinch immediately from higher gasoline costs and then secondary to that, higher refined product costs end up feeding through the supply chain and into our end-user purchases.” 

Ercolao said that Canada has navigated the trade dispute “fairly well” by diversifying trade in certain sectors, including shipments of energy products to Asia and Europe.

“That said, there’s still that acute pressure that’s being placed on very reliant industries in Canada on the U.S., especially in Central Canada like Ontario and Quebec with our steel industry, our aluminum industry and our auto industry,” he said.

Daniel Johnson, The Canadian Press

items.title: High Liner Foods to be bought by Umios in deal valued at $804 million
items.description: Nova Scotia seafood processor High Liner Foods Inc. says it has signed a deal to be bought by Japanese company Umios Corp. in an agreement valued at $804 million.
items._ogDesc: Nova Scotia seafood processor High Liner Foods Inc. says it has signed a deal to be bought by Japanese company Umios Corp. in an agreement valued at $804 million.
items.body:
LUNENBURG — Nova Scotia seafood processor High Liner Foods Inc. says it has signed a deal to be bought by Japanese company Umios Corp. in an agreement valued at $804 million.

Under the agreement, Umios, one of the world’s largest seafood companies, will pay $27 per share in cash.

High Liner shares closed at $15.08 on the Toronto Stock Exchange on Friday.

Umios plans to establish High Liner Foods as the core platform for its North American business, while maintaining its headquarters in Nova Scotia, the companies said.

  • Latest updates on company news here

The companies said Umios is committed to maintaining High Liner Foods’ workforce and operations, established brands and customer relationships.

“We ... are committed to preserving the heritage of this historic Nova Scotian and Atlantic Canadian business,” said a statement from Umios’ president, Daisuke Yasuda. 

Thornridge Holdings Ltd., which holds a 41.4 per cent stake in High Liner, has agreed to support the deal, which requires shareholder and other approvals. Several of High Liner Foods’ directors and officers who hold shares also support the deal, the company said.

Umios has operations in Japan, North America, Europe and Asia and is one of High Liner Foods’ long-standing suppliers.

High Liner Foods President and CEO Paul Jewer said Umios approached High Liner earlier this year and expressed interest in acquiring the company.

High Liner created a special committee from its board to consider its options, which included offers from Umios and a few other companies, he said. 

“We came to the conclusion that this was the best option for the company going forward,” he said. “It delivers significant value for our shareholders, but also we think creates wonderful opportunity for all of our stakeholders.”

High Liner Foods was founded in Lunenburg, N.S., in 1899 and is one of North America’s largest producers of frozen seafood products, selling its products in grocery stores and to restaurants and food retailers across Canada and the U.S.

High Liner employs about 300 to 400 people in Nova Scotia and about 1,300 across North America, Jewer said. He added that all of the company’s employees will keep their jobs.

“(Umios) committed to ... continuing to employ our people,” he said. “They’ve committed to continuing to operate our facilities, our plants and our offices. They’ve comitted to continuing to maintain our head office here in Nova Scotia.”

Shareholders are expected to meet in December to consider the transaction, which requires 75 per cent to vote in favour in order to be approved.

  • Latest updates on investing here

High Liner Foods’ board of directors unanimously recommended that shareholders approve the transaction, the company said.

In addition to Thornridge, Jewer said the other shareholders he has spoken to have expressed support for the deal.

“This is such a compelling deal for shareholders. We’re certainly looking forward to their support on the transaction,” he said.

The transaction will be implemented through a court-approved plan under the Nova Scotia Companies Act and is expected to close in early 2027.

Once the transaction is completed, shares, which trade under the symbol HLF, will be delisted from the TSX and High Liner will become a wholly-owned subsidiary of Umios, which is traded on the Tokyo Stock Exchange. 

By Tori Fitzpatrick in Halifax with files from Craig Wong in Ottawa

items.body:
Cole Smead, CEO & Portfolio Manager, Smead Capital Management

Focus: Canadian & Global Stocks

Top Picks: International Petroleum, Barclays, Autotrader

We remain convinced that the deeply out-of-consensus corners of the market, namely banks and energy, still have room to run, even after three years of leadership. The more interesting question isn’t whether these stocks have worked. It’s where they stand relative to where we bought them.

Take Cenovus. We bought into Husky Energy in December 2020 as it merged with Cenovus, when the combined company traded at roughly 40 per cent of invested capital. Back then, we needed to believe returns on capital could reach 10 per cent just to justify one time invested capital. Today, Cenovus trades near two times invested capital, and at current oil prices we estimate it’s producing closer to 30 per cent returns on capital. Returns could fall 40 per cent from here and the stock would still support that multiple. That’s a margin of safety the market still doesn’t appreciate.

We see the same dynamic in European banking. UniCredit traded below half of book value in 2022 as a high single-digit return of equity (ROE) business. Higher rates turned it into a mid-teens ROE business, and it now trades at a premium to book. We expect its purchase of Commerzbank to close, with further consolidation likely in Greece and Italy. Scale drives returns in capital-intensive industries, and the market is only beginning to price that in.

Our advice to investors: don’t confuse a stock’s three-year run with the end of its story. We’d rather be patient with what Mr. Market still doesn’t understand than chase what he already does.

items.body:
SAN FRANCISCO, U.S. - Microsoft is offering voluntary buyouts to about 60,000 employees, the company said on Monday, roughly a quarter of its workforce, as the tech giant seeks to cut costs while pouring money into artificial intelligence.

Staff on select teams in the United States, Canada, India and Britain at vice president level and below will be eligible, a Microsoft spokesperson said, while some groups of employees, including some working on data centers, sales and marketing, are excluded.

“The Voluntary Exit Offer reflects an important part of how we’re evolving our approach to change: creating greater flexibility and, where possible, more ways for employees to shape their next chapter,” Amy Coleman, an executive vice-president and chief people officer, told employees in a memo.

It’s the second voluntary buyout offer that Microsoft has offered employees this year.

In April, the company reportedly offered around seven per cent of its U.S. workforce the option to retire early.

Around 30 per cent of those eligible took the voluntary retirement plan, according to CNBC.

Microsoft had 223,000 employees globally at the end of June, down from 228,000 at the end of 2025, according to regulatory filings.

Around 27 per cent of Microsoft’s workforce is eligible for the new buyout offer.

The company is expected to report quarterly earnings later this week.

items.body:
CALGARY — Ovintiv Inc. is growing its Canadian holdings with its purchase of Logan Energy Corp. in a $1.26-billion deal, which includes the assumption of debt. 

The Denver-based company said Monday that the acquisition is expected to add about 20,000 barrels of oil equivalent per day of production in the Montney region, which stretches over parts of northern British Columbia and Alberta.  

The acquisition also includes two new oil batteries and interests in two natural gas processing facilities.

  • Stay on top of your portfolio with real-time data, historical charts and the latest news on oil

“This bolt-on transaction delivers value for our shareholders by adding high margin oil and condensate production and infrastructure, utilizing our operational advantage to drive significant synergies, and adding to our already deep drilling inventory and future growth optionality,” Ovintiv president and CEO Brendan McCracken said in a news release.  

“The Logan assets have demonstrated leading oil productivity performance and will immediately compete for capital alongside the rest of our portfolio.”

Ovintiv, formerly Encana, moved its headquarters to the United States from Calgary in 2020. It significantly increased its Canadian presence earlier this year, when it closed its $3.8-billion purchase of NuVista Energy Ltd., another Montney-focused player. 

  • How to set BNN Bloomberg as your preferred source on Google

Under the agreement announced Monday, Ovintiv will pay $1.40 per share in cash for Logan Energy. 

Logan Energy shareholders will also receive 0.0817 of a share in a new company, Logan Oil, plus 0.05 of a Logan Oil purchase warrant for each Logan Energy share they hold. Each whole warrant will entitle the holder to buy one Logan Oil share at an exercise price of $1 per share, within 60 days following the closing date.

The deal is expected to close early next year, subject to shareholder, court and regulatory approval. 

Lauren Krugel, The Canadian Press

VANCOUVER — Ksi Lisims LNG has finalized a deal to supply natural gas to German utility Securing Energy for Europe.

Under a binding sale and purchase agreement, SEFE is to buy one million tonnes per year of liquefied natural gas for 20 years, with deliveries set to begin in the early 2030s.

SEFE and Ksi Lisims signed an initial heads of agreement in May of this year.

  • Latest updates on commodities here

The project on the north coast of British Columbia near the Alaska border now has binding contracts for seven of its 12-million tonne per year capacity, and another two deals in the preliminary stages.

Houston-based Western LNG is the lead developer and future operator of Ksi Lisims alongside Rockies LNG, a consortium of Canadian natural gas producers, and the Nisga’a Nation, on whose lands the project would be located.

The $10-billion project has regulatory approval, and the partners have said they aim to make a final investment decision this year.

items.description: Former B.C. federal cabinet minister James Moore dissects David Eby's disastrous snap election gamble, arguing that British Columbians rejected political cynicism in favor of Lorne Doerkson's straightforward leadership.

items._ogDesc: Former B.C. federal cabinet minister James Moore dissects David Eby's disastrous snap election gamble, arguing that British Columbians rejected political cynicism in favor of Lorne Doerkson's straightforward leadership.
items.body:
James Moore is a former federal cabinet minister from B.C. under prime minister Stephen Harper and is a contributing columnist for CTVNews.ca.

VANCOUVER — British Columbians elected David Eby as their premier on Oct. 19, 2024. They elected New Democrat MLAs in 47 of 93 seats, giving his party a third term in government and a second consecutive majority government on that day.

He was given a majority mandate to govern until 2028 if he wanted to.

Speaking on election night, a freshly re-elected David Eby said to the assembled crowd: “The campaign is over, but the work has just begun, hasn’t it? I recommit myself. I know we all recommit ourselves to working for British Columbians every single day. That will be our sole focus: getting things done for British Columbians.”

He further added: “I know that British Columbians, our whole province, deserve a premier that is going to bring us together, not drive us apart. And I promise to be that premier, to bring British Columbians together.”

Less than two years into that four-year mandate, these two fundamental values asserted by the premier of British Columbia on election night would be shattered in a cynical snap election call by a desperate premier trying to take advantage of two perceived political opportunities: the B.C. Conservative Party, then in disarray, and the red-hot unpopularity of U.S. President Donald Trump and his vile presidency.

Where Premier Eby ultimately failed is that he presumed the voters were stupid. He presumed the voters would not see the obvious cynicism of his attempt to take advantage of the disarray of the Conservative Party. He presumed voters wouldn’t find that cynicism odious and unworthy of someone who held the office of the premier of the province of British Columbia.

He arrogantly assumed that British Columbians didn’t know that his government had a functioning majority government that had just passed the provincial budget and was cruising through the rest of the calendar year with a wafer-thin legislative agenda that would withstand any confidence vote for at least another six months, if not more.

He further assumed that voters were too dumb to understand that bilateral relations with the United States are largely led by the Government of Canada, not the premier of Canada’s third-largest province. And British Columbians, polls show, prefer the approach taken by Prime Minister Mark Carney to any evidence of an effort that has been proposed by Premier Eby.

  • More opinions and expert analyses

The public is smart about these things because the stakes are incredibly high, and we have been dealing with President Trump for a long time now. We know when there is a serious effort to protect Canadians and when people are just putting on a skit.

Premier Eby treated the public as though they were dullards who didn’t understand how our government works. He presumed that the public wouldn’t recognize crass politics when they saw it and that he could get away with a cheap electoral stunt to refresh his mandate and escape the coming collapse of his support within his own party.

Voters are smart, and they have an instinct for nonsense and insincerity when they see it. And they take great pleasure in holding accountable and punishing those who abuse the awesome privilege of serving in public office, to simply serve themselves in such a transparently dishonourable way.

Enter Lorne Doerkson

In the end, this whole exercise was doomed from the beginning, in part, because waiting for him on the debate stage was the new Conservative Leader, Lorne Doerkson. I imagine that at NDP headquarters, they have a hard drive somewhere with a dossier assembled on each of the 25 most probable B.C. Conservative leaders in the province, ready to go just in case one of those 25 people were to emerge as a leader for the party anytime soon.

I also imagine that the name Lorne Doerkson is not affixed to any of those 25 dossiers. Why? Because he is a leader, not like the others who we have seen in recent leadership campaigns.

He is a deviation, in a good way, from what politics has too frequently become. He isn’t a braggart. He isn’t a camera-hungry creature of the media. He isn’t somebody with a massive social media presence who obsesses about clicks and likes and thumbs up and subscribers and chatter. He isn’t a bomb-throwing partisan who lives off making people angry and stirring up irrational passions toward imaginary problems with unworkable solutions that entrench conflicts forever.

He’s a normal two-term MLA who was born in New Westminster, raised in Salmon Arm and lives in Williams Lake (population 11,000). He was a Rotary president and a rodeo announcer who was voted Williams Lake Stampede volunteer of the year in 2019. He spent 20 years working in local media at community newspapers in central and northern British Columbia, where he later became a financial planner before running for office in 2020.

He’s a humble, high-integrity, highly decent, hardworking, good guy who cares more about getting things done than being loved by pure ideologues or hated by those he disagrees with. In contemporary politics, he is an anti-hero of sorts to the overly righteous, overly loud crankiness of the noisy political norm.

In the face of David Eby’s cynical election call and divisive campaign of class warfare — which included a trashy and cheap attack on one of the greatest British Columbians we have ever known in the person of philanthropist Jimmy Pattison — Lorne Doerkson stood out as a refreshing new beginning for a province and a political culture in need of normalcy.

Turning the page

British Columbia has deep challenges, and the solutions won’t come easily for our new premier-elect. His new team, new caucus, new cabinet, and officials will wrestle with some of the biggest challenges that we have seen in our province in a generation. But the voters have sent a clear message that they want to turn the page on David Eby and the NDP and they offered Mr. Doerkson a massive mandate with seats across urban, suburban, and rural British Columbia to work together and get things done.

Premier Eby bet that British Columbians wouldn’t notice what he was doing with this election call. They noticed and fired him. For Lorne Doerkson, the work has just begun. If he governs as he campaigned, as a humble and thoughtful fixer of the myriad problems that the province faces, it will be a welcome fresh start for a province that so desperately needs one.

items.title: UNIQLO to open first downtown location at Pacific Centre
items.description: The Japanese retailer’s seventh B.C. location will join new Aritzia and Simons flagships in the former Nordstrom space
items._ogDesc: The Japanese retailer’s seventh B.C. location will join new Aritzia and Simons flagships in the former Nordstrom space
items.body:
UNIQLO will open its first downtown Vancouver store at CF Pacific Centre in spring 2027, marking the Japanese clothing retailer’s seventh location in B.C.

The Japanese retailer will join new Aritzia and Simons flagships to take up the space formerly occupied by Nordstrom. The three stores are scheduled to open between 2027 and 2028.

"UNIQLO’s new flagship store in Vancouver will bring its signature LifeWear philosophy to the heart of the city," said Cadillac Fairview, which owns and operates the shopping centre, said in a statement Monday.

In November 2025, Vancouver-based fashion retailer Aritzia announced plans for a four-level, 40,000-square-foot flagship boutique at CF Pacific Centre, with an opening initially targeted for 2027. Cadillac Fairview's latest announcement tentatively puts the opening in 2028.

Earlier this year, Quebec-based retailer Simons announced its plans to open its first downtown Vancouver store at the shopping centre. The approximately 92,000-square-foot location will span three floors and is scheduled to open in fall 2027.

“We are incredibly proud to support the growth of UNIQLO, Simons and Aritzia across Canada with these premier locations at CF Pacific Centre,” said Lillian Tummonds, senior vice-president of retail at Cadillac Fairview, in a statement.

“This major transformation reflects our shared commitment to creating unparalleled retail destinations, and we look forward to the energy and excitement these powerhouse brands will bring to the heart of downtown Vancouver.”

UNIQLO opened its first Canadian store at CF Toronto Eaton Centre in 2016, followed by its first B.C. location at Metropolis at Metrotown in Burnaby in 2017.

items.title: Bank of Canada now expected to hike key rate as it faces 'pivotal decision'
items.description: Expectations are rising that the Bank of Canada will indeed raise its benchmark interest rate this week as it considers the effect of higher energy prices on the economy.
items._ogDesc: Expectations are rising that the Bank of Canada will indeed raise its benchmark interest rate this week as it considers the effect of higher energy prices on the economy.
items.body:
Expectations are rising that the Bank of Canada will indeed raise its benchmark interest rate this week as it considers the effect of higher energy prices on the economy.

Financial market odds for a rate hike were just over 83 per cent as of Monday afternoon, according to LSEG Data & Analytics. The central bank's planned interest rate announcement on Wednesday will also include an updated monetary policy report.

The Bank of Canada has held its policy rate at 2.25 per cent for seven consecutive meetings.

RBC economists said in a note to clients Thursday that they are now expecting a quarter-point hike as the central bank faces a “pivotal decision amid evolving economic conditions.”

Last week, Statistics Canada reported the annual inflation rate rose to 3.1 per cent in September as the war in the Middle East continued to drive up gasoline prices. Excluding gasoline, the consumer price index rose 2.2 per cent year-over-year in September, easing from 2.4 per cent in August, suggesting higher energy prices haven't significantly spread throughout the economy yet.

Meanwhile, jobs data from StatCan released earlier this month showed the labour market stalled for a second month in a row in September as the economy lost 68,000 positions.

However, the RBC economists said they have “very low conviction” on a rate hike happening this week, and see a significant chance the Bank of Canada instead uses the meeting to set up a hike in December or January.

"While we don’t see an immediate need for the BoC to hike now, at the same time, a 25-basis-point increase in the overnight rate on Wednesday won’t materially change our medium-term economic outlook compared to a December or January hike," the note reads.

RBC assistant chief economist Nathan Janzen said in an interview that recent comments from Bank of Canada governor Tiff Macklem appeared to drive the change in expectations.

While speaking from the sidelines of the International Monetary Fund meetings in Bangkok, Macklem warned that persistently high global energy prices will drive up the inflation outlook at home.

“That essentially just emphasized that the central bank is increasingly worried about the potential impact of higher oil prices on future, broader inflation pressures, and they feel confident enough the economic backdrop is going to gradually continue to improve,” Janzen said.

The Bank of Canada released its latest business outlook survey last week, which suggested that business sentiment improved on average in the third quarter. However, it found that concerns remained about rising costs and the war in the Middle East.

"All the economic data that we've had to date is consistent with the view that the central bank, the Bank of Canada, was getting closer to raising interest rates," Janzen said.

Canadian interest rates are still relatively low, he added, and the neutral range — where rates are neither helping nor hurting the economy — sits between 2.25 per cent and 3.25 per cent.

TD Bank economist Marc Ercolao said in an interview that it is clear the Bank of Canada is becoming more concerned about the persistence of rising energy prices, "and that's what's starting to change the calculus."

While a hike is likely, he said there are also arguments for the bank to hold its key rate.

"There's interest-sensitive parts of the economy, particularly housing, that are already dealing with higher bond yields and too much additional tightening risks some unnecessary weaker demand in that space," Ercolao said.

"Overall, Canada's economy is growing, but it's not necessarily overheating by any means."

The impact of U.S. trade tensions on overall investment and a weakening labour market also support a decision to hold interest rates, he said.

He said a hike on Wednesday would be a risk management measure to prevent the inflation shock from becoming more persistent.

Ercolao said higher energy prices are a double-edged sword for the domestic economy.

"On one hand, higher energy prices are good for producers and government, and corporate revenue intake. It creates higher incomes especially in commodity-producing provinces," he said.

"But at the same time, it's households especially that feel the pinch immediately from higher gasoline costs and then secondary to that, higher refined product costs end up feeding through the supply chain and into our end-user purchases."

Ercolao said that Canada has navigated the trade dispute "fairly well" by diversifying trade in certain sectors, including shipments of energy products to Asia and Europe.

"That said, there's still that acute pressure that's being placed on very reliant industries in Canada on the U.S., especially in Central Canada like Ontario and Quebec with our steel industry, our aluminum industry and our auto industry," he said.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 26, 2026.

Daniel Johnson, The Canadian Press

items.title: Some Canadian homebuyers tune out tariff noise as trade war rumbles on
items.description: Ottawa broker says many clients are pushing ahead despite tariff uncertainty
items.content: <p>Ottawa broker says many clients are pushing ahead despite tariff uncertainty</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0373_639286291616924369.png" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: Ottawa broker says many clients are pushing ahead despite tariff uncertainty
items.body:
Geopolitical chaos and global economic uncertainty have stretched into 2026, pushing a hoped-for Canadian housing market recovery even further down the line as potential homebuyers wait for a calmer environment to emerge before making their move.

Bond market unease has sent five-year Government of Canada yields higher in recent months, pushing fixed mortgage rates upwards, while speculation is growing about at least one potential Bank of Canada rate hike in the months ahead.

Would-be buyers are still keeping a close eye on the latest political news – but while the announcement of US tariffs at the beginning of last year sent shockwaves around bond markets and hugely dented homebuyer confidence, a degree of acceptance has set in among mortgage shoppers about the trade war.

That’s according to Ottawa-based Smart Debt Mortgages broker Chris Allard (pictured top), who told Canadian Mortgage Professional many clients were still determined to push ahead with their purchase plans even with no end to the trade dispute in sight.

“I get the perception that people have largely tried to tune out some of the news and keep a positive mindset,” he said. “But there’s no doubt that everyone’s aware of what’s happening, and they’re aware that rates are rising and there’s significant concern for that.

“Now, the commentary that I often hear from borrowers, and this is true, is we see when Trump speaks now, the markets don’t automatically go up or automatically go down right away. And so that translates into the conversation that we’re having with our clients because they’re now recognizing that maybe it’s just a bunch of noise.”

Borrowers are still cognizant of the impact a big, unexpected development in the trade war would have for the economy and their plans – but they’re equally focused on making their mortgage work and optimizing their financial picture to move forward with their deal, Allard said.

“They’re trying to just look at their personal budget and try to make an educated decision based on the current environment rather than predicting if home values are up or down or rates are up or down,” he said. “They’re going, ‘What are my payments now? Am I comfortable now? And do I have a safety net?’”

BoC rate not expected to surge, even if a hike is on the way

Opinion is divided among leading economists on what’s in store from the Bank of Canada’s decision this Wednesday. Experts including Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation (CMHC) chief economist and senior vice president Mathieu Laberge don’t see a hike on the way yet, although Royal Bank of Canada (RBC) now marginally expects a 25-basis-point jump.

Most of the country’s top banks expect rate hikes to arrive at some point over the next year – but none are predicting the Bank of Canada’s benchmark rate, which strongly influences variable mortgage rates, will hit the highs seen in 2023-24.

That’s welcome news for borrowers, according to Allard. “I think a lot of Canadians might be surprised that the banks are not projecting significant prime rate increases,” he said. “It turns out that we did see fixed rate increases – and now it looks as though there won’t be significant prime rate increases.

“So I believe that just means that we might have more clients going into variable once they start to understand that dynamic.”

Clients focus on variable amid fixed-rate rises

Allard said he’s recently noted an increase in clientele wanting variable rates with a static payment amid a wider move away from fixed rates. “Bank of Montreal [BMO] offers that, TD Bank offers that, there’s a few others that offer it,” he said.

“Borrowers are [saying] ‘Well, maybe I can benefit from a rate in the high threes, have a stable payment, even though I’m taking a variable-rate product.’ It’s a really interesting move that we’re seeing from a consumer behaviour standpoint.”

items.title: District Energy Wants The Mechanical Room (And To Give Your Rooftop Back)
items.description:
Every residential tower gives up part of itself to equipment. From early plans, mechanical systems typically claim a room in the basement and a penthouse on the roof (the latter being prime real estate, mind you). This approach means that square footage is spoken for before the first suite is laid out.

Developers pay to build that space, but can’t sell or rent it. And today, with construction costs high and interest rate hikes back on the table, that cost is increasingly difficult to absorb.

“For developers building today, trying to make their projects pencil, taking capital off of traditional real estate development is a major factor,” said Diego Mandelbaum, Chief Development Officer at Corix, which builds and runs district energy systems as a utility across North America. “Reducing square footage for inefficient, building-scale mechanical space is a major piece of that, because doing so translates into both more usable area, and cost savings for developers.”

District energy moves thermal equipment out of individual buildings. In short: a central plant, usually located somewhere on, near, or below a project site, produces heat and chilled water for cooling and sends it through a network of pipes to every building connected to it, so the buildings themselves don’t need their own boilers. And because all of that energy is made in one place, the plant can switch to cleaner sources over time, like waste heat captured from a nearby power plant or wood waste that would otherwise go to landfill. This type of system has been around for well over a century — Corix’s district energy network at Ohio’s Cleveland Thermal dates back to 1894, for example — and now, the same central-plant model is helping today’s developers get space and capital back.

And those capital gains aren’t only about reclaimed square footage. Sometimes, they’re connected to meeting standards that are as well-meaning as they are costly. The starting point for the district energy system co-developed by Corix at Oakridge Park in Vancouver was a municipal low-carbon building policy. Meeting it tower by tower would have been an expensive effort — both in space and in capital. But that wasn’t the only way.

“At Oakridge Park, our solution was to rip out the mechanical equipment from each individual tower and centralize it. That allowed the development to meet the City’s green zoning requirements while saving a tremendous amount of capital and space,” Mandelbaum explained. At buildout, Oakridge Park will reach about 5 million square feet.

Oakridge Park (via Corix)

The savings can reach a project’s financing, too. CMHC is the only provider of mortgage loan insurance for multi-unit residential properties in Canada, and much of the country’s new rental housing is financed through it. And, CMHC-insured loans carry efficiency and sustainability requirements that are expensive to meet when approached one building at a time.

“We’re able to help developers meet these standards,” Mandelbaum says. In so many words, Corix can unlock financing solutions on a developer’s behalf, clearing a path to the CMHC-insured loans a project needs.

The earlier Corix is brought into a project, the more of those savings there are to find, since the team can help shape a master plan’s massing before plant spaces and penthouses get locked in. But no matter when the partnership is formed, the developer doesn’t carry the cost of the plant and pipes; Corix does, recovering that investment over the long term through the rates its customers pay for energy.

That means keeping those rates competitive comes first, and building too much, too soon would push them up. Which puts the pressure on timing.

“District energy doesn’t really work by just looking at an engineering study and asking, 'Can we make it work?' It’s about figuring out how to phase in your generation, and your capital, lock-in-step with the development," Mandelbaum said. "It's also about understanding that a developer will never give you certainty on how long it’ll take to build things out, because the market will never give you certainty."

So Corix builds in phases, leaning on modular construction and prefabrication to add capacity as buildings come online. At UniverCity, the residential community beside Simon Fraser University (SFU), work started with modular natural gas boilers while the community grew. Once the system had enough load, made possible by connecting SFU’s Burnaby campus, Corix invested in a much larger biomass plant, which burns wood waste otherwise bound for landfill. Today, the system heats the university and its neighbours, spanning nearly 5 million square feet in total.

Burnaby Mountain District Energy Utility near Simon Fraser University (via Corix)

Utah City, a sprawling master plan south of the border, is following the same path. There, Corix came into the picture after the first building was already up. Waiting on the grid wasn’t really an option: the development would have needed about 70 megawatts of power for its thermal systems, Mandelbaum explained, and the local utility would have needed 10 years to supply it.

Understandably, the developer had some questions about implementing district energy. But with construction in progress, the development team had tangible, tendered prices for mechanical equipment in hand, and could check Corix’s numbers against them directly. Spoiler: they held up.

“We built a modular plant in Washington state, we put it on a truck bed, we got it to site as soon as possible, and we got things energized within two years of the handshake,” Mandelbaum said.

Today, about 20 million square feet of real estate is set to be served by the system. Once enough of it is connected, Utah will see its own version of SFU’s switch: Corix will capture waste heat from a ~1.3-gigawatt gas-fired power plant about a mile away, which currently vents that heat into the atmosphere.

“What we're doing is closing the loop on what’s otherwise a wasted resource,” Mandelbaum explained.

Developments like these can take decades to build out, but Corix can handle a waiting game, thanks in large part to its ownership structure. The company is wholly owned by British Columbia Investment Management Corporation, which manages public pensions in British Columbia.

“We’re able to take a very long-term view," Mandelbaum said. "We have patient capital."

Utah City (via Corix)

That long view extends to everyone a system touches. Before a shovel goes in the ground, Corix looks at each project from every stakeholder’s side: the developer, the regulator, the municipality and, ultimately, the customer.

For Mandelbaum, the approach comes down to one question: “How’s a customer going to feel and experience this?”

And for the people who’ll call these communities home, the payoff lives in space reclaimed at the lower level, or on the sun-soaked rooftop.

“Just imagine," Mandelbaum said, "if every single rooftop was able to be used for amenity space. Or for recreation. Or for a garden."

items.title: Rising demand for multigenerational living reshapes B.C. home design
items.description: More than half of B.C. residents would consider multigenerational living, new RBC survey finds
items._ogDesc: More than half of B.C. residents would consider multigenerational living, new RBC survey finds
items.body:
More B.C. families are exploring multigenerational living to help younger generations enter the housing market amid affordability challenges, a trend that is influencing how homes are designed and built.

More than half (54 per cent) of British Columbians said they would consider living in a multigenerational home, the highest results among Canadian provinces, according to a Royal Bank of Canada (RBC) survey released earlier this month.

Among B.C. homeowners, 38 per cent said they would sell their home and buy one with their child to help them enter the market, also the highest regional result.

“In the last year and a half, I would definitely say that we have had an uptick at our company of inquiries,” said Suraj Jhuty, co-principal of Theorem Developments, a Vancouver-based multiplex and laneway house builder.

Many parents who own property in Vancouver and have adult children struggling to enter the housing market are now looking to redevelop their single-family homes into multiple units for family members to live in, he said.

The boutique firm is now working with four clients who plan to redevelop their single-family homes into four- to six-unit properties, with each family member occupying a unit.

“We are kind of getting out of this early adoption phase and a lot of families are seeing multiplexes come up in their areas,” Jhuty said.

Bryn Davidson, co-founder of Vancouver-based design and build company LaneFab, said his team has also seen growing demand for multigenerational homes in B.C., following the introduction of more flexible zoning requirements in some municipalities.

“First they allowed basement suites and then they allowed laneway houses and then they started allowing duplexes,” Davidson said.

“There are more options for people to build multigenerational housing on their own properties.”

The ability to create separately titled units, with their own financing arrangements and the flexibility to be sold independently, is appealing to families, he added.

“Laneway houses and multiplexes are spreading to other cities, you're starting to see broader interest in something that's been happening in Vancouver for a very long time,” Davidson said.

The trend extends beyond single-family properties, with some developers in Metro Vancouver incorporating multigenerational living into townhouse and condo designs through lock-off units.

These units within a townhouse or an apartment typically have separate entrances and full kitchen and bathroom facilities. One example is Juno, a condo development in Surrey that offers lock-off layouts.

“What I see in 2026 [is that] multigenerational living is not the same as the traditional model, where everyone eats at the same table every day,” said Inge Roecker, an associate professor at UBC’s School of Architecture and Landscape Architecture.

“It is more about creating shared spaces but everyone still has a totally private space.”

Benefits go beyond finances

Roecker said multigenerational living can do more than help families navigate affordability challenges in the region. It can also foster a more connected lifestyle that is common in many cultures and countries, and offer social and health benefits.

“Canada always says we are multicultural and then when I look at how we build, there is nothing multicultural,” Roecker said. “We traditionally build single-family homes and people are expected to fit into that family model.”

Families who want to live with their extended relatives, including those from South Asian countries where multigenerational households are more common, often have limited housing options. The same applies to single people who want to remain close to their families while maintaining their own living spaces, she said.

“We know now how much energy it takes to single something out, and the same goes for zoning…it’s a very unnatural thing and takes a lot of effort and energy to keep it up,” Roecker said.

“I totally welcome that we're finally looking at different models and how we create either your own family or families coming in all shapes and sizes in the 21st century.”

Multigenerational living can also allow young parents to go out occasionally without worrying about their children, as grandparents living next door can help with child care. Older adults may also benefit from having their children close by, according to Roecker.

About 73 per cent of Vancouver seniors aged 65 and over are homeowners, according to 2021 census data from Statistics Canada.

“We have no way to relocate all these people so we have to figure out [a way],” Roecker said.

In addition to laneway houses, duplexes and lock-off units, some developers are exploring housing complexes with shared courtyards where residents can gather and socialize, according to industry insiders.

“It's a newer phenomenon here in North America, but when you go to Europe, it is fairly recognizable,” said Jhuty, noting that his team is working on projects where multiple units share access to a courtyard.

Fragment House, a social housing proposal developed by students at UBC’s School of Architecture and Landscape Architecture, is an example of a design centred on shared spaces. The proposal includes a courtyard, a public café and a flexible studio for residents intended to foster social connections.

Roecker said the growing popularity of multigenerational living and higher residential density also require infrastructure and neighbourhood amenities to keep pace.

“We can have more stores, more cafés sprinkled in [neighbourhoods], we can have really nice bike paths and connect the [urban] fabric way better,” she said. “We can make the communities way more vibrant. … That’s my vision.”

items.description: Durham broker says younger and older clients alike are rejecting AI-generated video on social media
items.content: <p>Durham broker says younger and older clients alike are rejecting AI-generated video on social media</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0373_639283724664853667.jpg" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: Durham broker says younger and older clients alike are rejecting AI-generated video on social media
items.body:
Artificial intelligence has been a gamechanger for the mortgage industry – but somewhat paradoxically, the rise of AI solutions is pushing plenty of mortgage brokers to find ways to amplify the human touch and focus on the value they can provide separate from ChatGPT and Claude.

For Sherry Corbitt (pictured top), a mortgage broker with Mortgage Architects in Ontario’s Durham region, that’s translated into building a social media presence on the principle that authenticity wins.

Short-form video content has become an increasingly prominent part of her marketing strategy, Corbitt told Canadian Mortgage Professional, in an approach that’s been influenced by the growing aversion of many Canadians to AI-generated slop.

Younger generations, Corbitt’s assistant told her, are not into watching videos created by AI. “They just want authentic,” Corbitt said. “They want the ums and ahs. They want somebody to just do quick, genuine stuff.”

She also works on a significant volume of reverse mortgages, a product that naturally skews toward older, Facebook-active clients, and has noticed those generations are equally resistant to AI content – for a good reason.

“They’re scared of what’s fake,” Corbitt said. “So if they want to deal with you, then you have to be authentic and do your own videos.”

A recent CIRA (Canadian Internet Registration Authority) survey revealed that over half (53%) of Canadians encountered fake content generated by AI in the past year, up from 34% in 2025 and 20% in 2024.

And a Harris Poll Canada poll found that nearly nine in 10 Canadians are concerned about deceptive online content generated by AI, while a Roku Video-on-Demand Evolution study found that four out of five Canadians believe the use of AI in advertising should be labelled.

Industry pushes back on AI-generated advice

Mortgage industry members have also flagged the potential risks posed by AI mortgage misinformation for potential homebuyers.

Real Estate and Mortgage Institute of Canada (REMIC) founder and chief executive Joe White told CMP that AI “has a wonderful ability to give you an answer that sounds incredibly confident, but in many cases it’s the fine details that it gets wrong because it’s trained on everything out there on the internet – accurate information as well as inaccurate information.”

Other industry executives, including broker Angela Calla, say they’ve utilized AI for back-office workflow, but avoid it entirely for client conversations.

“We use it as a personal business resource to refine communication, strengthen our standard operating procedures, and improve efficiency,” Calla told CMP. “We don’t use AI to communicate directly with clients.”

How to jump on the authentic-content train

There’s no magic number for daily video output – Corbitt targets multiple a day, although she said each video typically focuses on addressing only one person, covering one topic, and answering one question.

That’s a formula she says creates a near-unlimited supply of material, as well as removing the production pressure that puts many brokers off starting.

Aside from knowing how to record and upload videos to social media platforms, Corbitt highlighted that the approach doesn’t require a huge amount of digital know-how. “I’m not tech savvy at all,” she said. “So being able to use just a few easy programs where you can do your subtext and things like that – it’s going really well. I’m enjoying it.”

New video content has helped Corbitt’s authenticity shine through, she said, as well as increasing brand awareness among first-time buyers and the cohort of Canadians who encounter mortgage advice while passively scrolling.

“I’m having success with my realtor partners who are dealing with first-time buyers… and the videos, I think that helps, too,” she said. “Because they’re watching the videos. So I’m not having a problem with that market.”

items.title: FCAC report highlights often hidden or hard-to-find bank fees
items.description: A sizable fee pool and costly account switching put competition in the spotlight
items.content: <p>A sizable fee pool and costly account switching put competition in the spotlight</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0373_639286120868796948.png" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: A sizable fee pool and costly account switching put competition in the spotlight
items.body:
Bank fees that look small one at a time can be hard to see, predict and compare, the Financial Consumer Agency of Canada (FCAC) said in a review released Friday. It added that the costs can add up over time, especially for lower-income Canadians.

The 130-page A Review of Banking Fees in Canada, requested by Ottawa in Budget 2025, looked at fees on personal deposit accounts, not mortgages. Across nine fee categories, financial institutions earned an estimated $2.45 billion in 2025, the Globe and Mail reported.

Where costs get hidden

FCAC said multiple fees can apply to a single transaction, foreign exchange and cross-border debit fees can be embedded in a purchase price, and usage-based fees are hard to predict when customers cannot track their transactions.

FCAC’s backgrounder also flagged multiple fees on one ATM withdrawal, excess transaction fees, and prepaid product fees that can erode balances over time. It said point-in-time disclosures do not always show cumulative costs.

The review said customers with lower incomes, less savings or heavier reliance on daily banking may be disproportionately affected, CBC reported.

“Canadians should be able to clearly understand what they are paying for banking services. When fees make the full cost harder to see, it affects both affordability and competition,” FCAC commissioner Shereen Benzvy Miller said in the release. “More transparency makes it easier for consumers to compare options and save money, and financial institutions have stronger incentives to compete for their business.”

Switching, competition and open banking

The review also pointed to barriers to switching. Transfer-out fees raise the cost of moving an account, and customers face indirect costs such as time and paperwork. “We need financial institutions to remove the friction for switching,” Benzvy Miller said in an interview with the Globe. Canada’s six largest banks together hold more than 90% of the market, the Globe reported.

FCAC said consumer-driven banking, also known as open banking, could make fees more visible and help consumers compare and switch providers. The Consumer-Driven Banking Act received royal assent in March. Proposed regulations published in June place the framework under the Bank of Canada’s oversight. It would let people share their financial data with accredited providers of their choice.

The mortgage industry has long advocated for open banking, CMP has reported.

The Canadian Bankers Association (CBA) did not directly address the findings in its response. CBA chief executive Anthony Ostler said in a statement: “When money is put in a bank in Canada, deposits are insured and the bank is overseen by regulators who ensure Canadians are treated fairly and their money is secure.”

What it means for brokers

The review does not examine mortgage products. But everyday banking costs shape clients’ monthly cash flow, and brokers who want to discuss total cost can point clients to FCAC’s Account Comparison Tool and the low-cost and no-cost account commitment the agency supervises.

items.title: Expect 50bps of BoC hikes by January, says Oxford Economics
items.description: Oil-driven inflation, a weakening job market and fragile housing complicate brokers’ rate outlook
items.content: <p>Oil-driven inflation, a weakening job market and fragile housing complicate brokers’ rate outlook</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0373_639286119071177242.png" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: Oil-driven inflation, a weakening job market and fragile housing complicate brokers’ rate outlook
items.body:
Oxford Economics now expects the Bank of Canada to raise its key rate by a cumulative 50 basis points by January 2027, about a year earlier than it projected in September, as surging oil prices push inflation higher.

The forecast lands days before the central bank’s Oct. 28 decision, with the overnight rate at 2.25%. Oxford expects 25-basis-point hikes on Oct. 28 and in December, returning the rate to what it estimates is a neutral 2.75%. It does not view the moves as “the start of a tightening cycle.”

Markets have moved toward a hike. A Reuters poll of economists conducted Oct. 21-23 found 19 of 34 (56%) expect a quarter-point increase to 2.50% next week and another by the end of March. Overnight swaps implied about a 75% chance of an October hike, according to Bloomberg data.

Oil lifts headline inflation, not yet core

Consumer prices rose 3.1% year over year in September, up from 3.0% in August, with gasoline up 27.8%, CMP reported. The Bank’s preferred core measures, CPI-trim and CPI-median, averaged 1.9%.

Oxford expects headline inflation in the mid-3% range in late 2026 and early 2027. It assumes Brent crude stays above US$100 a barrel for the next six months. Oil hit $117 a barrel on Oct. 23, Reuters reported.

Governor Tiff Macklem has grown more wary. Speaking at IMF meetings in Bangkok, he warned that “the risk that inflation broadens and becomes more persistent has gone up,” RBC economist Abbey Xu noted.

Others see less urgency. Dominion Lending Centres chief economist Sherry Cooper said last week: “Today’s inflation report reinforces our view that higher gasoline prices temporarily boost headline inflation while further eroding household purchasing power. However, these energy-driven increases, largely tied to geopolitical tensions, are unlikely to trigger a broader resurgence in underlying inflation.”

Oxford, too, expects slack and slower shelter inflation to keep core inflation from rising sharply. Still, it called the October decision “a toss-up” after softer jobs and inflation data, adding: “even if it doesn’t hike in October, we still anticipate it’ll lift the overnight rate by a cumulative 50bps by January.”

Housing and household debt in focus

Statistics Canada said the economy lost 68,000 jobs in September, lifting unemployment to 6.5%. Oxford trimmed its 2027 GDP growth forecast by 0.1 percentage points to 1.3% and left 2026 at 1.0%. It projects the 10-year government bond yield near 4% through 2027, a key input for fixed mortgage pricing.

On housing, the report said: “We expect home sales volumes and prices to slide this fall and into early next year as mortgage rates rise.” It added that elevated debt “will continue to constrain spending by Canadian households and make them vulnerable to job losses, higher interest rates, and a resurgence in oil prices.”

Trade remains a drag. The US imposed 50% tariffs on C$27.6 billion of Canadian goods effective Aug. 22, and Canada countered from Sept. 8, according to a Finance Canada statement.

Oxford warned that if oil prices don’t ease in 2027, the Bank could “hike rates to the top of its neutral range at 3.25%, or even higher into restrictive territory.”

For brokers, the Bank will release updated inflation projections alongside the decision. Variable-rate clients feel any hike through prime, while renewals face fixed pricing set by bond yields. Both groups may need early conversations about payment tolerance and rate holds.

items.description: Mortgage renewals, a softer job market and the Nov. 5 budget loom over a cautious outlook
items.content: <p>Mortgage renewals, a softer job market and the Nov. 5 budget loom over a cautious outlook</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0373_639286117374425429.png" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: Mortgage renewals, a softer job market and the Nov. 5 budget loom over a cautious outlook
items.body:
Parliament’s budget watchdog has cut its 2026 growth forecast to 0.9% and projects federal deficits above $63 billion through 2030-31, citing a new round of US tariffs and Canadian countermeasures.

The Parliamentary Budget Office (PBO) released its Economic and Fiscal Outlook last week. It now sees real GDP growth of 1.5% in 2027, down from 1.1% for 2026 and 1.6% for 2027 in June. The PBO estimates that trade measures in place since early 2025 could shrink the economy by about 1.4% over the medium term if they become permanent.

That change arrives just ahead of the next Bank of Canada decision, with economists currently divided on whether the central bank will hike rates or hold steady. 

The PBO assumes the Bank of Canada starts raising its policy rate early in 2027 and reaches a neutral 2.75% by mid-year. It stressed this is a projection assumption, not advice on monetary policy. Markets are pricing in something sooner. A Reuters poll found 19 of 34 economists expect a quarter-point hike on Oct. 28.

For households, the PBO flagged that consumption could prove weaker than projected as those “renewing mortgages taken out when interest rates were lower face higher payments, leaving less income for other spending.” It also expects residential investment to recover from a 2026 decline, helped by new federal housing measures and borrowing costs well below their 2023-24 peak.

“Canada faces a more challenging economic and fiscal outlook than we projected in June,” parliamentary budget officer Annette Ryan said. “Additional trade measures and ongoing uncertainty are weighing on growth in real output – what we produce as a country.”

Jobs, inflation and the rate path

The PBO expects unemployment to rise to 6.7% by the end of 2026 as employment falls faster than the labour force. Its figures predate Statistics Canada’s September report, which showed 68,000 jobs lost and unemployment at 6.5%.

Inflation should average 2.8% in 2026, driven by higher energy prices tied to disrupted shipping through the Strait of Hormuz and by pressure from Canada’s countermeasures.

Deficits and the Nov. 5 budget

The PBO projects a $63.3-billion deficit in 2026-27, down from $71.8 billion in its June outlook. It then sees the shortfall peaking at $70.2 billion in 2027-28 and easing to $67.8 billion by 2030-31. New measures, including $36 billion for the Productivity Mega Deduction and $7.5 billion in tariff support, cost $52.6 billion over five years. That more than offsets $37.4 billion in additional fiscal room from stronger revenues.

Public debt charges are the fastest-growing federal expense, rising from $59.3 billion in 2026-27 to $83.0 billion by 2030-31. Federal debt per person is projected to climb from $33,436 to $39,191 over the same period. A permanent 100-basis-point rise in rates would add $5.1 billion to debt charges in the first year.

The PBO expects Ottawa to meet its operating-balance anchor in 2028-29, but not its goal of a declining deficit-to-GDP ratio. “A balanced operating budget anchor should not be interpreted as a balanced fiscal position,” Ryan said. “By design, it excludes debt-financed capital spending, meaning borrowing and debt can continue to grow while the target is being achieved.”

Finance minister François-Philippe Champagne said the budget, due Nov. 5, will “outline the next steps in our plan to build a stronger, more resilient and more affordable Canada,” The Canadian Press reported. The PBO’s numbers do not include measures from that budget. It judges risks to its outlook as roughly balanced, with trade policy the dominant uncertainty.

For brokers, the report is a prompt to revisit renewal scenarios with clients, particularly those in trade-exposed work, before the Bank’s decision and the budget land.

items.title: FSRA moves to refuse renewal of mortgage agent’s licence
items.description: Regulator cites past conduct and false licence information
items.content: <p>Regulator cites past conduct and false licence information</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0373_639286114617501801.png" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: Regulator cites past conduct and false licence information
items.body:
Ontario’s financial services regulator has proposed refusing to renew the licence of mortgage agent Anna Angelidis, alleging her past conduct and false information on a licence application make her unsuitable to be licensed.

The Financial Services Regulatory Authority of Ontario (FSRA) announced the notice of proposal Friday. The allegations have not been proven. Angelidis has requested a hearing before the Financial Services Tribunal.

FSRA says Angelidis is not suitable to hold a licence under the Mortgage Brokerages, Lenders and Administrators Act, 2006 and its regulations. It alleges her past conduct gives reasonable grounds to believe she will not deal or trade in mortgages lawfully, honestly and with integrity. It also alleges she provided false information on a licence application.

The regulator’s announcement did not describe the conduct in question. It also did not say which licence level Angelidis holds, which brokerage authorized her, or when a hearing might take place.

Suitability under scrutiny

The case fits a broader push by FSRA to police who is fit to hold a licence. When it released its final licensing suitability guidance in July 2024, Huston Loke, FSRA’s executive vice-president of market conduct, said: “This is the first time we’re releasing guidance that explains how we assess if someone is suitable to hold a licence, strengthening sector practices and further protecting Ontarians working with mortgage professionals.”

FSRA’s guidance says the regulator may refuse, restrict, suspend or revoke a licence if it has reasonable grounds to believe someone is unsuitable. It also says oversight of agents and brokers is a brokerage’s ongoing responsibility.

Recent notices have turned on similar questions. In a December 2025 notice, FSRA alleged that a Level 2 agent answered “No” on a renewal application when asked whether he was under investigation. A March 2026 notice proposed refusing another agent’s renewal in a case FSRA framed as a test of suitability. Those cases are separate from Angelidis’s, and the hearing requests in each remain unresolved.

What happens next

A notice of proposal is not a final decision. In a 2025 case, CMP reported that FSRA may proceed with its proposed order if no hearing is requested within 15 days of receipt. Because Angelidis requested one, the Tribunal will review the proposal.

For brokers and principal brokers, the case is a reminder that FSRA can assess suitability at renewal, and that the accuracy of what is submitted on licensing forms is part of that assessment. Brokerages may want to confirm that their screening and supervision processes match FSRA’s published expectations.

items.title: B.C. Conservatives win majority government, CTV News declares
items.description: David Eby’s snap election gamble has handed the B.C. Conservative Party a majority government, CTV News has declared.
