items._ogDesc: David Eby’s snap election gamble has handed the B.C. Conservative Party a majority government, CTV News has declared.
items.body:
David Eby’s snap election gamble has handed the B.C. Conservative Party a majority government, CTV News was first to declare Saturday night.

While some ridings have yet to be called, interim leader Lorne Doerkson’s party secured more than enough seats to relegate the B.C. NDP back to the Opposition benches after nine years in power.

The Conservatives were leading or elected in 62 of the province’s 93 ridings when he made his victory speech to a roaring crowd.

“Our best days are still ahead of us, my friends,” Doerkson said. “We are going to super-charge British Columbia.”

In a conciliatory address, the premier-designate from Williams Lake vowed to represent rural and urban communities alike, and to work with the province’s First Nations.

“This future is one that we will build together as partners, with all the certainly all of us need,” Doerkson said.

He did not directly reference his campaign pledge to repeal B.C.’s Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples Act.

The winner did reiterate the party’s plan to triple B.C.’s liquefied natural gas production by 2035, and its promise to provide a $1,000 tax cut for nearly every worker—while also maintaining and improving the province’s strained public health system.

“I want a B.C. where a hard day’s work gets you a family home and a future, right here in this beautiful province,” Doerkson said.

Eby resigns as NDP leader

Earlier, in a somber concession speech before NDP supporters, Eby announced his resignation as party leader.

“This is obviously something I do with a very heavy heart, but it is time for new leadership within our party,” he said.

“It has been a wild ride, but my family has paid a very significant cost for this work, and I am very keen to spend some time with my kids, with my wife, with our friends—and not worry if someone is videotaping me while I am singing karaoke.”

He also reflected on some of the NDP’s accomplishments, which included more than $7 billion invested in school capital projects, the elimination of Medical Services Plan payments, and increasing the minimum wage from among the lowest in Canada to the highest of the provinces.

Eby has also credited his government’s short-term rental restrictions and forced housing density policies for helping to bring down what had once been skyrocketing rents.

“We should all be proud of that,” he said. “It has been the honour of my life to serve as premier.”

But his decision to send voters to the polls two years into his mandate—following weeks of Conservative infighting and defections—will go down as a historic blunder, said political scientist Stewart Prest.

“Nobody in the province wanted him to do this,” Prest said on the eve of the election.

“He alone ultimately bears responsibility for the NDP having two fewer years in power than they were scheduled to have, and I think that is going to leave a mark on his legacy.”

Despite leading the party to defeat, Eby was re-elected in his Vancouver-Point Grey riding.

The next leader of B.C.

Premier-designate Doerkson has been the MLA for Cariboo-Chilcotin since 2020, but only became interim Conservative leader 34 days ago, following predecessor Kerry-Lynne Findlay’s resignation.

For many voters, he was a blank slate contrasted with the baggage Eby carried into the campaign.

Prior to entering politics, Doerkson’s resume included newspaper publisher, financial planner, Rotary president and rodeo announcer. A younger Doerkson also competed in bareback riding, which left him with broken bones and a dislocated shoulder.

“I have watched a lot of people get thrown at a rodeo, and I’ll say I’ve been thrown a few times myself,” Doerkson told the crowd in his victory speech.

“You pick up yourself, dust yourself off, and you get back on—and the crowd gets to its feet for you because you’re trying. That is the approach that I have brought to my political life.”

Doerkson and the Conservatives were elected despite repeated NDP warnings that the party offered a political home for candidates and staffers with extremist views, including some separatist sympathies.

  • B.C. Conservatives dump candidate accused of making Hitler remarks

Over the course of the campaign, the party ejected two candidates—Joachim Agou and Jordan McIntosh—over offensive social media posts, though both were running in NDP strongholds.

Doerkson notably stood behind campaign director Katy Merrifield even after a social post emerged in which she called Islam an “abhorrent ideology.”

After Eby forced the Conservatives into a campaign without a permanent leader, the NDP raised questions about whether Doerkson would be able to serve as premier long-term—as the party’s constitution mandates a leadership race within the next year, and bars interim leaders from running.

The Conservative board of directors responded to those concerns with a statement last month assuring the constitution would be amended for Doerkson, should his campaign succeed.

“A premier chosen by British Columbians deserves the certainty of leading his party. This amendment will provide it,” the statement added.

Such an amendment would require a two-thirds vote—in a party that has been plagued by infighting since nearly clinching victory in 2024.

Party in turmoil pulled together

When Eby called the election, a schism had been forming on the province’s political right.

The Conservatives suffered an exodus of MLAs over the summer, each citing problems with then-leader Findlay, whose divisive rhetoric led to charges of playing “Trump-style politics.”

The trouble continued into mid-September, when allegations emerged that a former executive director for the Conservatives had hired a private investigator to snoop on the party’s critics, both internal and external.

“I was unaware of it,” Findlay said at the time. “I can’t really respond. They are just allegations.”

Shortly after, eight former Conservatives banded together under CentreBC, a fledgling party billed as a more moderate alternative free from radical affiliations.

  • Conservative defectors join CentreBC, with Peter Milobar named leader

Findlay ultimately resigned amid mounting calls for her to step aside—and growing speculation of Eby’s snap election intentions.

The premier pushed ahead with the call two days later, only to see his political opponents announce their reunification within hours.

The snap election interrupted what could have become an “increasingly institutionalized division” on the right side of the political spectrum, Prest said.

“This is another piece of David Eby’s legacy,” he said. “He essentially did the one thing that could bring these different factions of conservatism back together again in the province.”

Prest, an associate professor of political science at the University of British Columbia, also argued the reunification should have been easy to predict.

“You can’t say no one could possibly have known the Conservatives would put aside their differences to fight an election because that’s exactly what happened in the run up to the 2024 election,” he said.

Seven members of CentreBC returned to the Conservatives on the day the writ dropped, leaving only Elenore Sturko, who became the party’s leader.

She was defeated Saturday in her Surrey South riding.

Conservative platform

Doerkson’s party notably did not provide a costed platform in time for the B.C. leaders’ debate, or the first days of advance voting.

The plan the Conservatives ultimately presented promised to reduce the province’s expected $14-billion deficit to $10.8 billion over three years, based on economic growth forecasts significantly higher than those included in B.C.’s latest budget.

Ahead of the election, Doerkson defended the most ambitious prediction—of 3.2 per cent GDP growth in 2029—as “absolutely doable,” despite skepticism from some economists.

The interim leader also managed to overcome NDP-fanned fears that a Conservative government would be disastrous for public health care, particularly given his pledge to “never raise taxes.”

  • ‘Absolutely doable’ or ‘wishful thinking’? Doerkson defends costed platform

Prest argued it’s going to be hard for the party to make good on its promises.

“The province’s economic situation has deteriorated and a good chunk of that is outside the control of any premier, given those trade winds buffeting the country right now,” he said.

“It’s hard to claim to be fiscally responsible and also invest in all the kinds of social care and health care that British Columbians are rightly demanding and the Conservatives are promising. At some point, the rubber is going to hit the road.”

The party further promised to expand $10-a-day childcare, fund 500 more RCMP officers to be deployed to rural areas over five years, hire 50 more Crown prosecutors, and expand the use of involuntary care.

The Conservatives’ environmental platform was largely tied to massively increased LNG production, with the party suggesting the expansion would reduce global greenhouse gas emissions by replacing higher-emission fuels used in Asia and Europe.

items.body:
Time for your cheat sheet on this week’s top stories.

Canadian Real Estate

Canadian Real Estate Prices To Fall Even Further: Oxford Economics

The Canadian housing crash is already the largest on record, and it may not be over. Oxford Economics is forecasting prices and sales falling further through early 2027. Higher rates, elevated energy prices, and weak job growth threaten a recovery. The housing market is seen improving next year, though the firm warns the risk is still to the downside.

Canadian Mortgage Growth Slumps As Rate Hikes Threaten More Pressure

Canadian mortgage credit is slowly growing, and BMO warns it can slow further. Mortgage debt grew 0.3% in August, the second-slowest growth for the month on record. Annual growth was also the weakest since the early 2000s, excluding the recent correction. With roughly 30% of originations in Q2 2026 opting for variable rates, BMO cautions the Bank of Canada (BoC). Hiking too fast can hit a growing share of borrowers and throttle mortgage demand.

Canadian Real Estate Needs More Immigration, Foreign Buyers: National Bank

A whole generation of young adults want to buy a home but can’t afford it. They were pitched on the idea that more supply can fix that, but it turns out that’s not the case. Over 28% of completed new homes remain unsold, the highest level since the 90s. Unfortunately, prices are still out of reach for buyers, and National Bank says the show must go on. They’re urging policymakers to increase immigration and permit foreign buyers to boost demand.

Canada’s Borrowing 2.2x Deficit, Payments To Hit 1 in 7 Dollars of Revenue: PBO

Canada’s Parliamentary Budget Officer (PBO) warns the country’s debt demand is rising. Canada’s 5-year deficit is projected to hit $333 billion, but it needs $733 billion new borrowing—2.2x the deficit. It’s the result of a “growing stock of debt,” not rising interest rates, according to the PBO. Debt servicing is now the fastest-growing federal expense, with payments soon to consume 1 in 7 dollars of revenue.

Canadian Inflation Accelerates, Only 2 Provinces Below National CPI

Energy and shelter costs are helping to drive the Consumer Price Index (CPI) higher. Annual growth of CPI accelerated to 3.1% in September, surpassing the 3.0% upper bound used by the BoC. The headline is high, but just two provinces are lower than the national average. The rest are facing much higher CPI levels, especially in Atlantic Canada.

Toronto Real Estate

Toronto New Home Sales Rise, But Remain Weak As Price Declines Accelerate

Toronto’s new home sales climb but remain weak. September’s new home sales came in 63.9% higher than last year, but they remain 52% below the 10-year average. Most of those sales were single-family homes, where prices plunged 12.7% (-$180.8k) over the past four months. Condos haven’t fallen as much, but sales were the lowest for September on record. Even with taxpayers providing billions in incentives, the market is still struggling.

Halifax Real Estate

Halifax Real Estate Prices Just Made The Second-Biggest Drop On Record

The Halifax-Dartmouth real estate market may have finally run out of luck. The price of a typical home in the region plunged 3.9% (-$22.1k) in September, marking the second-biggest monthly drop on record. Sales came in 4% hgiher than last year, but they remain well below pre-pandemic volumes. The region has so far avoided the turmoil seen in Toronto and Vancouver, but last month’s sharp drop shows the region isn’t in the clear.

items.title: Northern B.C. housing market holds relatively steady as local economy recovers
items.description: The region’s home sales in the third quarter was 3.9 per cent below historical averages
items._ogDesc: The region’s home sales in the third quarter was 3.9 per cent below historical averages
items.body:
Northern B.C.’s housing market is holding relatively steady compared with other parts of the province, supported by a recovery in the local economy over the summer, according to the BC Northern Real Estate Board (BCNREB).

The board reported 1,009 seasonally adjusted residential sales in the third quarter of 2026, down 3.1 per cent from the same period last year and 3.9 per cent below historical averages.

The average sale price across the board’s region reached $464,180, up 0.1 per cent from the previous quarter.

“In comparison to other board regions in B.C., the North most closely follows its historical average sales levels, hovering between four to eight per cent below that benchmark across the past few quarters,” the BCNREB said in a release published earlier in October.

The board said the relative stability "has corresponded with a resurgence in the local economy over the summer, with our nowcast measure of Northern economic growth now closely following its provincial counterpart after a largely contractionary 2025.”

Much of this recovery is attributable to “robust” employment growth in the North Coast and Cariboo areas, according to the BCNREB.

Prince George recorded the most sales in the region in the first nine months of the year, with 1,043 properties worth $531.4 million changing hands, a 2.1 per cent decline from the same period last year. Fort St. John followed, with 541 properties worth $244.9 million sold, down 3.6 per cent year-over-year.

“The sales-to-active listings ratio remained largely flat from the previous quarter, hovering near 18.2 per cent, keeping Northern markets near the upper threshold of balanced conditions,” the board said.

Looking ahead, the BCNREB warned that inflationary pressures and rising bond yields have pushed five-year fixed mortgage rates above five per cent, potentially limiting housing demand.

Taking into account current national economic and labour market conditions, markets were also anticipating further Bank of Canada interest rate increases in 2027, according to the report.

“Despite these headwinds, we continue to expect sales activity in the North to outperform the rest of B.C., underpinned by relatively better affordability conditions,” said the board.

items._ogDesc: Halifax home prices posted their second-largest monthly dollar drop on record as September new listings hit a six-year high, despite rising sales.
items.body:
Greater Halifax real estate may be running out of luck. Canadian Real Estate Association (CREA) data shows a six-year high for new listings in September. Sales also rose, but couldn’t prevent the second-largest monthly price drop on record.

Halifax Home Prices Post Second-Largest Monthly Drop On Record

The price of a typical home sold through the MLS across Halifax-Dartmouth.

Source: CREA; Better Dwelling.

Greater Halifax home prices fell sharply last month. The price of a typical home dropped 3.9% (-$22.1k) to $541,700 in September, leaving prices 4.1% (-$23.4k) below last year. In dollar terms, it was the second-largest monthly drop on record, only beaten by the May 2022 plunge after rate hikes began. Prices are now 5.4% (-$31.0k) below the May 2026 record high, bringing them to their lowest level since December 2024.

Home Sales Rise But Remain Below Pre-Pandemic Volumes

Halifax-Dartmouth home sales through the MLS in September.

Source: CREA; Better Dwelling.

Existing home sales rose but remain tepid. A total of 434 homes sold in September, up 4% from last year but still well below pre-pandemic levels. Rising sales aren’t an obvious driver of falling prices, but volumes remain weak—and look worse against elevated inventory.

Halifax New Listings Hit A Six-Year High For September

Halifax-Dartmouth new listings of homes for sale in September.

Source: CREA; Better Dwelling.

September isn’t traditionally a big month for sellers, but last month was an exception. CREA reported 727 new listings in September, up 1.4% from last year. That increase looks modest next to sales growth, but new listings have climbed for four years straight. Last month saw the highest September volume since 2020.

Halifax-Dartmouth has largely resisted the price declines dragging down the national benchmark. However, that resilience was based on a relatively small pool of buyers. Thin sales leave prices vulnerable when those buyers pull back or when sellers face more competition. With listings rising and prices falling sharply, the market may now be testing where buyers are willing to step in.

items._ogDesc: Companies controlled by billionaire B.C. property developer Terry Hui allege that the Canada Revenue Agency has engaged in a "pattern of misconduct" in its attempts to collect on ballooning tax debts dating as far back as 2007.
items.body:
Companies controlled by billionaire B.C. property developer Terry Hui allege that the Canada Revenue Agency has engaged in a "pattern of misconduct" in its attempts to collect on ballooning tax debts dating as far back as 2007.

Five companies within Hui's real estate development group are targeted in the audit by the CRA, including Adex Securities, One West Holdings, a B.C. numbered company and two Luxembourg-based shell companies.

The companies filed an application in Federal Court this month, claiming the government has wrongfully moved to collect on tax debts totalling more than $200 million, most of which is accrued interest.

The application says the group is involved in capital-intensive real estate projects in Toronto, Vancouver and Calgary and the audit, initiated in 2013, focused on transactions that relied on Canada's tax treaty with Luxembourg.

The companies say in the application that they've received tax debt assessments this year, with Adex owing $45 million and interest of more than $65 million, while the two Luxembourg based companies owe together more than $92 million and $127 million in interest.

One of the companies' lawyers said in a statement that the total debt being sought by the CRA is approximately $219 million, due to "overlapping liabilities" between the entities.

The companies want the court to stop the government from collecting on the debts until a related case filed earlier this year is concluded, while objecting to the CRA wanting $115 million security payment from Adex.

Requiring a payment that large and not allowing the company to defer will cause the real estate group to "lose significant capital that is currently being used to fund active development projects."

The application is one of at least three filed in Federal Court this year related to the dispute, where they claim that being forced to pay will cause "irreparable harm" and that no advance notice from the CRA means that they "could not have reasonably planned for a debt … of this magnitude."

The companies claim the revenue agency has exhibited a "pattern of misconduct," alleging its officers acted outside established policies and procedures and "without regard to the impact of their actions on taxpayer businesses."

Lawyers for the companies were not immediately available for comment, but Justin Kutyan with KPMG Law in Toronto told The Canadian Press earlier this year that the transactions in the case were similar to a tax structure upheld by the Supreme Court of Canada in 2021.

The court ruled 6-3 in favour of Alta Energy Luxembourg, which had claimed a tax exemption on a capital gain of more than $380 million under Canada's treaty with Luxembourg, described in the decision as being "well known as an international tax haven."

The court found in Alta's favour, ruling that Canadian tax authorities couldn't use anti-tax avoidance rules to "judicially amend or renegotiate a treaty."

The dissenting justices in the case, however, said "the federal government did not deliberately set out to create the conditions for unlimited tax avoidance by means of schemes" used by the company.

The dissenters wrote that "the court should not legitimize such blatantly abusive tax avoidance based on the view that Canada should have negotiated different treaty terms."

The CRA said it did not have a spokesperson available for an interview to comment on tax treaty abuse.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 21, 2026.

Darryl Greer, The Canadian Press

items.title: Canadian Real Estate Prices To Fall Even Further: Oxford Economics

Oxford Economics expects Canadian home prices to fall further as rising mortgage rates, weak hiring, and stretched valuations weigh on demand.

The post Canadian Real Estate Prices To Fall Even Further: Oxford Economics appeared first on Better Dwelling.
items._ogDesc: Oxford Economics expects Canadian home prices to fall further as rising mortgage rates, weak hiring, and stretched valuations weigh on demand.
items.body:
Canadian real estate is already in its largest correction on record by some measures, but it may get worse. A new Oxford Economics report forecasts further declines in home prices and sales as rising interest rates hit an already weak market. High energy prices, economic uncertainty, and stretched valuations are expected to add further downward pressure.

Canadian Home Prices And Sales Expected To Fall Further

Despite the severe correction in home prices, the firm sees them moving lower for at least a few months. “We expect home sales volumes and prices to slide this fall and into early next year as mortgage rates rise,” explains Tony Stillo, director of Canada economics at Oxford Economics.

He notes that home prices remain elevated relative to incomes, presenting further risk for homebuilders. Rising expectations of rate hikes add to that risk.

Bank of Canada Rate Hikes Expected Soon

The firm expects two rate hikes from the Bank of Canada (BoC) by the end of this year, the first within days. Next week they see a 25 basis point (bp) hike at the central bank’s October 28th meeting, and another in early December. Next week’s hike may be delayed by the recent weak employment data, according to Stillo. But he still sees a 50 bp increase by January, bringing the overnight rate to 2.75%, their estimate of neutral, where monetary policy neither stimulates nor throttles economic activity.

As economists are increasingly noting, the driver of rate hikes here isn’t an overheated economy. Weak economic and employment data reinforces that this isn’t an economy firing on all cylinders, but one that would struggle with rate hikes. However, Stillo explains the catalyst fueling rate hike expectations is energy prices.

Brent crude is forecast to remain above US$100 per barrel for six months, he notes. By their calculations, this is expected to push headline inflation into the mid-3% range in late 2026 and early 2027. Bond yields have already begun to reflect expectations of upward pressure.

“A rapid rise in bond yields will continue to push borrowing costs higher throughout the economy, weighing on interest-sensitive sectors like housing and spending on consumer durables,” warns Stillo.

Weak Hiring and a Shrinking Population Add To Housing Pressure

Higher interest rates won’t be the only factor working against housing activity in the near-term. “A weak job market weighed down by the ongoing trade war with the US, squeezed household incomes from high fuel prices, and a shrinking population will hurt housing demand,” explains Stillo.

He cites the 68,000 jobs lost in September—roughly 110,000 lost over the past two job reports—as evidence that hiring will remain weak over the short-term. A perfect storm of higher fuel costs squeezing disposable income, tariffs, and trade uncertainty is weighing on businesses.

Canada’s population declines are a less certain factor. Stillo expects the population to decline if policymakers maintain their goal of shrinking the share of non-permanent residents (NPRs) to 5% of the population by the end of 2027. The recent upward revisions suggest a much sharper decline would be needed to meet that goal. Oxford is awaiting Ottawa’s immigration update before revising its demographic forecast.

As for weaker households, they face a sticky situation. Higher rates will squeeze spending power, but so would higher energy prices and elevated inflation. “Elevated debt will continue to constrain spending by Canadian households and make them vulnerable to job losses, higher interest rates, and a resurgence in oil prices,” warns Stillo.

Oxford doesn’t see the downturn lasting forever—it only feels that way. The firm expects a housing recovery to start in the second half of 2027 through 2028, just a little over a half-decade since the correction began. Before then, rising borrowing costs and weak demand point to a near-term slump. However, with prices still stretched relative to incomes, Oxford warns the correction could prove deeper or longer than its baseline forecast.

items.title: Markham's Nearly-Complete EverHome Condo Project Placed Under Receivership
items.description:
Another development project that’s nearing completion has become insolvent, according to filings in Ontario Superior Court — the latest in an extensive list of projects that are struggling to cross the finish line.

The project is EverHome, by Toronto-based developer The Sher Corporation, and is located at 9704 McCowan Road in Markham near the intersection with Bur Oak Avenue, just north of the Williamstown Plaza shopping centre.

For the site, The Sher Corporation is developing a mid-rise condo project with 131 units across three buildings, plus an amenity building.

For the project, The Sher Corporation — through Sher Markham Inc. and Sher Holdings Inc. — secured financing from Meridian Credit Union in July 2022 for a construction demand facility in the amount of $57,251,849.81, with interest accruing at Meridian’s Prime Rate + 1.75% per annum (with an all-in floor rate of 4.20%), plus a letters of credit facility in the amount of $1,100,590.40.

According to court filings, 103 of the 131 units — 78.6% — had been pre-sold as of July 2026. Construction was approximately 86% complete before halting in May 2026.

Construction Halts

“Construction on the Project halted in or around mid May 2026 due to reported safety concerns identified by the safety consultant, resignation of the construction manager, compounded by a funding gap and associated cost overruns,” said Meridian in an October 7 application seeking to place the project under receivership. “As at that date, the Project’s structures were substantially completed, building envelopes were near completion, and the interior works were incomplete and behind schedule.”

According to Meridian, the construction manager raised several safety issues in May 2026 to Shakeel Walji — the President and corporate director of The Sher Corporation, as well as the guarantor of the loan — including “numerous serious safety deficiencies and non-compliance items onsite, including hazards, fire safety concerns and unsafe stair access conditions, noting many of the items required immediate corrective action.”

The construction manager, Grove Inc., then terminated all work in light of the safety concerns.

A rendering of the EverHome project. (The Sher Corporation)

Eastpointe Corp. was retained as the new construction manager in July 2026, and worked with the project cost consultant, CB Ross Partners, to conduct an assessment and prepare an updated construction budget. They concluded that, as of July, the cost to complete the project was around $17.3 million, a dated number that is now expected to be larger.

According to Meridian Credit Union, The Sher Corporation has defaulted on the loan agreement on several occasions, including by failing to provide financial statements, failing to repay the loan by September 2025, failing to repay the loan by March 2026, and failing to fund cost overruns.

The Receivership

Meridian said it issued a formal demand for payment in August 2026 and gave the developer until August 17 to repay the loan. The Sher Corporation was unable to do so, and Meridian subsequently also learned that the developer had $58,650.48 in insurance premiums that were past due, which Meridian then paid in September.

Meridian says it was owed $57,731,133.87 as of September 15, 2026, with interest continuing to accrue. The lender also says that the developer has not provided a solution to address the outstanding debt and has also allowed 21 liens totalling to $11,422,954.19 to be registered against the property.

According to the lender, Walji reached out in July 2026 to explore the possibility of seeking out creditor protection under the federal Companies’ Creditors Arrangement Act (CCAA).

According to an affidavit sworn by Walji on October 13, The Sher Corporation secured $21,150,000 in debtor-in-possession (DIP) financing from Safe Harbour Global Capital to fund the potential CCAA proceeding. Walji said the financing “provides a proposed means of addressing the immediate funding shortfall that has prevented the Sher Project from being completed” and “this new new capital would preserve the value of the substantial work already completed and avoid the value destruction and additional cost that could result if construction remains incomplete or is interrupted for an extended period through a receivership proceeding.”

Meridian’s receivership application was scheduled to be heard by the court on October 14, and Walji asked for an adjournment of 30 days so they can finalize the CCAA application and DIP financing. However, the judge presiding over the case ultimately sided with Meridian.

“There is no viable CCAA option, there is real risk to the security of Meridian in waiting further and nothing but speculative chances of delay producing more than a deeper hole to dig out of,” said Judge Sean Dunphy, who added that “the very fact that Meridian prefers to take its chances in a receivership now rather than later speaks volumes as to how viable that particular DIP proposal is.”

Meridian’s receivership application was then granted, and the project is now under receivership as of October 14.

items.title: Construction costs, policy certainty top B.C. builders' priorities ahead of B.C. election
items.description: Industry groups urge the next government to lower costs, improve transparency and strengthen coordination
items._ogDesc: Industry groups urge the next government to lower costs, improve transparency and strengthen coordination
items.body:
With the B.C. election approaching, builders across the province say they want the next government to address rising construction costs and provide greater policy consistency for the industry.

Improving the predictability of the project pipeline, transparency around how development fees are spent and communication among different levels of government are also among the priorities that building industry associations want the next government to address.

“Reducing the cost to build is felt right across the province,” said George Greenwood, CEO of the Canadian Home Builders' Association of BC (CHBA BC).

“The cost to acquire the land and then building materials, labour costs, these are all contributing to making homeownership more out of reach for average British Columbians.”

CHBA BC is calling for streamlining approval processes, reforms to the municipal infrastructure funding model and greater municipal transparency and accountability in how they calculate, collect and spend fees charged to developers.

The organization is also calling on the next government to pause potential mandatory changes to the province’s energy step codes, which set progressive energy-efficiency requirements for new construction in B.C. Greenwood argues it would add more costs to builders.

“We're just saying take a more stable approach, even putting it on a pause, let people catch their breath,” he said. “The economy is not strong right now. The housing market is not strong.”

The Vancouver Regional Construction Association (VRCA) is also urging the next government to look at ways to reduce charges imposed on developers and increase transparency on how the revenue is spent.

“The additional fees added to housing from development cost charges and other charges are not helping get housing built, not to mention all the other impacts of what's happening in the economy and interest rates,” said Jeannine Martin, president of VRCA.

“[We also want to see] more transparency on what's happening with that, what that's paying for, and how we are utilizing that to build housing.”

Chris Atchison, president of the BC Construction Association, said he also wants greater government transparency, including the reinstatement of the Major Projects Inventory reports, which was discontinued late last year.

Atchison said recent policy discussions, including a proposal to convert vacant condo units in designated growth areas into affordable homes using financing through Build Canada Homes and BC Housing, and a two per cent tax on vacant residential properties, have raised concerns about mixed policy signals to the construction industry.

“We need policy consistency and a predictable project pipeline. They're critical to housing delivery,” said Atchison.

“Because construction is a long-term industry, all of our projects can take years to plan, to finance, to approve and deliver, so businesses need confidence that the policy environment will remain stable throughout that process.”

Those who spoke with Business in Vancouver said they also hope to see better communication among different levels of government, saying there is still room for improvement, and continued investment in skilled trade training programs.

items._ogDesc: Canadian mortgage credit growth posted its weakest August since 2013. BMO warns renewed rate hikes could add pressure to borrowers.
items.body:
Canadian borrowing is losing steam just as interest rate hikes come back into focus. Bank of Canada (BoC) data shows mortgage credit posted its smallest August increase since 2013, pushing annual growth to a pace rarely seen outside housing corrections. With nearly a third of new mortgages carrying variable rates, renewed tightening could further throttle slow activity.

Canadian Mortgage Debt Growth Slows To Weakest August Since 2013

Canadian household debt: Residential mortgage credit, annual growth rate.

Source: Bank of Canada; Better Dwelling.

Residential mortgage debt advanced 0.3% (+$7.1 billion) to $2.45 trillion in August. That was unusually slow, marking the smallest August increase since 2013. Annual growth decelerated for a tenth straight month, leaving the balance only 3.8% (+$89.1 billion) higher than last year. It’s a slump that’s catching the attention of at least one Big Six economist.

“In August, household mortgage debt grew just 3.8% y/y, the slowest pace since the worst of the housing correction in 2023-24 (and before that, since the early 2000s),” explained Shelly Kaushik, senior economist at BMO Capital Markets.

Ontario & BC Slump, Weak New Condo Demand Slows Growth

The weak credit growth serves as a reminder that market stabilization isn’t the same as normalization. While the national market is stabilizing, it’s masking the prolonged slump in BC and Ontario. Weak demand in these regions, along with weak new condo demand in general, “has kept a lid on the recent recovery in borrowing,” according to Kaushik.

The data highlights another area the Bank of Canada (BoC) may be watching, explains Kaushik. “Canadian monthly credit aggregates, which typically fly under the radar, highlighted an ongoing slowdown in the economy’s most interest-rate-sensitive sector just as the Bank of Canada may be looking more closely at raising rates.”

Rate Hikes May Add To Mortgage Payment Stress

Bond yields are surging higher, but housing demand remains relatively weak. “Suffice it to say the housing market isn’t exactly in need of extinguishing,” says Kaushik. Variable-rate loans accounted for roughly 30% of new mortgages in Q2, according to BoC data cited by BMO, leaving those borrowers exposed to renewed rate hikes.

“Indeed, a new tightening cycle could add payment stress to variable rate mortgage holders,” she warns. Mortgage borrowing is already struggling to regain momentum. Renewed tightening could add further pressure to both the recovery and the households carrying that debt.

items.title: Could inflation fears push the Bank of Canada toward its first hike since 2023?
items.description: RBC economists flag near-even chance of a rate jump or hold
items.content: <p>RBC economists flag near-even chance of a rate jump or hold</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0388_639282903689072151.png" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: RBC economists flag near-even chance of a rate jump or hold
items.body:
The Bank of Canada enters its October 28 rate decision at a crossroads, with Royal Bank of Canada (RBC) economists projecting a 25-basis-point hike to the overnight rate, the first since 2023. But Frances Donald, Chief Economist at RBC in Toronto, and Nathan Janzen, Assistant Chief Economist at RBC, are not confident.

“We have very low conviction on the idea of a rate hike this soon, and it’s almost equally probable the central bank uses this meeting to tee-up a coming hike in December or January,” they wrote in an October preview.

Crucially, the RBC team is not calling for a hike on urgency grounds.

“Our expectation of a move higher from the BoC on Wednesday is not because we believe there is an urgency to hike interest rates,” Donald and Janzen wrote.

Instead, they attribute it to a shift in the Bank’s communication since its September 2 decision, which they read as signalling a preference to act preemptively against inflation rather than wait for it to materialise.

The case for patience remains strong. Canada’s labour market lost 68,300 jobs in September, its worst month of 2026, lifting the unemployment rate to 6.5%.

August gross domestic product is expected to have risen just 0.1%, below Statistics Canada’s 0.2% advance estimate.

Five-year Government of Canada bond yields have nonetheless climbed more than 40 basis points over three months, while West Texas Intermediate (WTI) oil has averaged US$95 per barrel since the last BoC decision, 54% above year-earlier levels.

Sherry Cooper of Dominion Lending Centres Group says underlying inflation trends remain consistent with a wait-and-see approach, while Stéfane Marion of National Bank of Canada expects the Bank of Canada to refrain from hiking rates next week. https://t.co/7HWcvP53Lr — Canadian Mortgage Professional Magazine (@CMPmagazine) October 20, 2026

Divided views on whether a rate hike is warranted

Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation (CMHC) chief economist and senior vice president Mathieu Laberge, addressing the Mortgage Professionals Canada (MPC) National Conference in Calgary on October 18, was unambiguous.

“I don’t see rates going up anytime soon,” Laberge said.

“Governor Macklem was really, really clear that he has no tools to do anything about global inflation. He could kill the economy as much as he wants, and kill domestic inflation, but current inflation is coming from supply chain disruption and oil prices due to war in Ukraine and the Strait of Hormuz.” 

Laberge placed his base case firmly beyond this year.

“The economy is not extremely [strong] right now. We saw the labour market numbers,” he said.

“So my hunch right now is: not before 2027. Our previous forecast was mid-2027. We may bring that forward a little, so maybe end of Q1, early Q2 2027, but I don’t see anything this year.” 

Douglas Porter, chief economist at BMO Capital Markets in Toronto, acknowledged the divided outlook.

“If anything, the threat of higher inflation has rekindled chatter of a potential rate hike in 2026,” Porter said.

“We still view that as a very long shot indeed, with the economy struggling to grow, core inflation moving closer to the 2% target, and USMCA uncertainty still clouding the outlook.” 

What the October 28 decision means for mortgage brokers

Donald and Janzen argue a 25-bps move on Wednesday would not materially alter the medium-term economic picture – their base case already assumes 100 basis points of rate increases in 2027.

For brokers, what matters more is the forward guidance that accompanies it.

“Rather than the rate hike itself, we will be monitoring for any communication that helps us understand the Bank of Canada’s expected path of interest rates ahead,” they wrote.

The RBC economists offer a broader signal that mortgage professionals should not ignore.

“Central banks do not have the same patience for inflation they might have had in the past, and are willing to act preemptively to guard against it,” Donald and Janzen wrote.

For professionals navigating Canada’s ongoing mortgage renewal wave, Laberge’s remarks underscore that portfolio risk endures regardless of Wednesday’s outcome.

“The renewal shock may be easing for some households, but the risk has not vanished,” he said.

“It has moved. It’s sitting in existing portfolios. It’s more regionally concentrated than it’s ever been, and the resale conditions are softer.” 

Adding to the complexity, the Bank will deploy Prima, its new forecasting model that places mortgage renewals at the centre of the rate-setting framework, at its October meeting for the first time.

“No model is going to solve every problem, but we are hopeful that this model will be better suited for a world with more supply shocks and in a more interconnected world,” Macklem told reporters in September.

Whether it sharpens the Bank’s read on supply-driven inflation will become clear Wednesday.

items.description: Glasslake Funding’s Doug Robinson: FINTRAC non-compliance is a risk brokers can no longer ignore
items.content: <p>Glasslake Funding’s Doug Robinson: FINTRAC non-compliance is a risk brokers can no longer ignore</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0388_639282884379552081.png" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: Glasslake Funding’s Doug Robinson: FINTRAC non-compliance is a risk brokers can no longer ignore
items.body:
With additional reporting by Fergal McAlinden

Two years after mortgage brokers became reporting entities under Canada’s anti-money laundering framework, a senior industry voice is sounding a warning: the window for wilful inaction has closed.

Doug Robinson of Glasslake Funding, a Toronto-based alternative mortgage lender, drew on a dual background in policing and lending to take stock of where brokerages stand on compliance.

Robinson was speaking at the Mortgage Professionals Canada conference in Calgary, two years on from October 11, 2024, the date on which the Financial Transactions and Reports Analysis Centre of Canada (FINTRAC) brought mortgage administrators, brokers and lenders under the Proceeds of Crime (Money Laundering) and Terrorist Financing Act (PCMLTFA).

“I can pretty much guarantee this will not blow over,” Robinson said.

“If you’re a broker or owning a brokerage and you haven’t done any work on FINTRAC stuff, you may want to.”

Robinson described two camps that emerged when the rules were first announced: those who hired compliance staff, documented policies and prepared in earnest, and those who hoped the requirements might quietly disappear.

As the debate over challenging FINTRAC requirements for brokers rumbles into 2026, Robinson argued the regulator’s baseline expectations are more achievable than commonly assumed.

“FINTRAC doesn’t want mortgage brokers to become experts in reporting money launderers,” he said.

“They just wanted to add mortgage brokers because you guys are governed by a regulator and you have an obligation, and it fortifies Canada’s anti-money laundering landscape.”

Know your client — or know the risk

Robinson anchored his anti-money laundering (AML) framework around three questions every broker must be able to answer: who is the applicant, how will they service the mortgage, and where did the down payment come from? The third, he said, is the most exploited vulnerability in the transaction chain.

“In lending and in mortgages, the down payment is usually, in my opinion, the softest spot,” Robinson said.

“If someone’s looking to get a whole bunch of money into the system in one spot, they’ll usually do it through down payment.”

He urged brokers to build what he called “reasonability statements” — documented explanations that account for the origin of funds — warning that gift letters alone carry limited evidentiary weight.

“The reasonability statements go a long way,” he said. 

Policies, risk ratings, and a lender blind spot

Robinson outlined five elements every brokerage should have in place:

  1. a designated compliance officer or administrator
  2. written policies
  3. a company-level risk assessment
  4. AML training — leverageable through MPC for smaller shops
  5. a completed two-year self-assessment

 A smaller brokerage, he noted, can assign compliance responsibilities to an administrative staff member, provided the function is kept separate from the sales side.

His sharpest criticism was aimed at lenders. “In my opinion, lenders are soft on being concerned about where the repayment comes from,” Robinson said.

Accelerated or lump-sum payments made after funding, he argued, too often pass without scrutiny, a gap that sophisticated money laundering schemes are positioned to exploit.

Robinson also flagged British Columbia’s unexplained wealth orders (UWOs), a civil mechanism under the province’s Civil Forfeiture Act that can compel individuals to account for assets exceeding $75,000 that appear disproportionate to their known income, all without requiring a criminal conviction.

Some mortgage professionals argue that regulation is both burdensome and necessary. Robinson, a former police officer, sits firmly in the latter camp. He suggested the UWO model could spread beyond British Columbia as the courts test its constitutional limits.

“There’s no downside to reporting an unusual transaction report to FINTRAC,” he said.

“Sometimes big investigations start from a really small report that someone put in sometime.”

items._ogDesc: GTA new home sales rose in September but remain historically weak. Single-family prices plunged $180k in four months, while condo sales hit a record low.
items.body:
Greater Toronto Area (GTA) new home sales picked up in September, but the recovery remains shaky. BILD and Altus Group data shows sales rose 63.9% from last year, but they remain historically weak. The bigger story is prices—nearly a third of the single-family correction has occurred in the past 4 months. New condo prices have held up better, but buyers are balking with sales hitting a record low for the segment.

Toronto New Single-Family Homes Fell $180k In The Past 4 Months

The Altus Group benchmark price of single-family and condo apartment homes across Greater Toronto.

Source: Altus Group; BILD GTA.

New home prices continued to slide, led by single-family homes. The segment’s benchmark slipped 0.2% (-$2.1k) to $1.25 million in September, down 13.3% (-$190.7k) from last year. September’s decline was modest, but the bigger story is the sudden return of plunging prices.

Prices have effectively fallen off a cliff since May, dropping 12.7% (-$180.8k) in just four months. That accounts for nearly 95% of the decline over the past year. The benchmark is now 35.5% (-$687.1k) below its July 2022 record high. The percentage decline over the past four months alone is more than a third of the total decline from the peak, leaving prices where they were almost 6 years ago.

New condo prices have held up much better. The segment’s benchmark fell 1.0% (-$10.3k) to $1.03 million in September, just 0.2% (-$1.7k) below last year. Prices are now 17.6% (-$220.9k) below the March 2022 record high—roughly half the percentage decline seen in single-family homes. That relative strength has narrowed the price gap between the two segments to just $215.2k. Whether that means single-family homes are now relatively weak or new condos are set to correct further is anyone’s guess. However, a breakdown of home sales suggests demand for new condos at these prices is almost non-existent.

New Home Sales Rise, But New Condo Sales Hit A September Low

Greater Toronto new home sales in September.

Source: Altus Group; BildGTA; Better Dwelling.

New home sales jumped, but the above chart should temper expectations. There were 949 units sold in September, up 63.9% from last year. Single-family homes accounted for 820 sales, the strongest September since 2021. Condos weren’t so lucky: just 129 units sold, down 40.3% from last year and the weakest September on record.

The increase is welcome, but a base effect makes it sound more impressive than reality. Despite the jump, total sales remained 52% below the 10-year September average. Sales of single-family homes have recovered, while condo demand continues to find new lows.

New Home Inventory Falls, But Remains Elevated

New home inventory fell but remains lofty by the region’s historical standards. There were 19,957 new homes for sale in September, down 8.2% from last year. Despite falling below the past two years, inventory remains at its third-highest September level since 2015. New home inventory might be lighter, but relative to sales, this remains a weak demand balance.

Toronto’s new home sales improved, but the numbers are less impressive when broken down. Single-family sales picked up alongside steep declines in prices. As for condos, prices are firmer, but with sales at record lows, buyers are balking at those prices. Last month’s numbers are even less impressive when one considers it’s the result of billions in bailout programs. From developer bailouts to tax incentives, that’s a lot of public support for a market struggling to find buyers.

items.title: Slower homebuilding risks wiping out Canada’s affordability gains, economists warn
items.description: The national housing market may be sluggish, but the lacklustre pace of housing construction could worsen affordability problems
items.content: <p>The national housing market may be sluggish, but the lacklustre pace of housing construction could worsen affordability problems</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0373_639282861144967017.jpg" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: The national housing market may be sluggish, but the lacklustre pace of housing construction could worsen affordability problems
items.body:
Canada’s housing market has been mired in a years-long slump, pushing prices lower amid plunging demand – but economists still say the sluggish pace of homebuilding could worsen the affordability crisis in the long run.

Mathieu Laberge (pictured top), chief economist and senior vice president at Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation (CMHC) and Stéfane Marion, chief economist and strategist at National Bank of Canada, sounded an ominous note on the construction outlook during speeches at the recent Mortgage Professionals Canada (MPC) National conference in Calgary.

Laberge highlighted how the slower pace of construction in 2026 could have significant negative consequences for the market down the line.

“Our latest housing supply report points to the central issue: right here, right now across Canada, construction is slowing faster than the underlying need for housing,” he said. “If we react to a softer market by stopping too much construction, we may be protecting ourselves from today’s risks – but we’re also creating tomorrow’s shortages.

“We are at a very high risk that by not providing the appropriate and sufficient supply today, we will lose the improvement in affordability we’ve seen two or three, or five years down the road.”

Residential construction continues to slide

The Canadian Real Estate Association (CREA) recently revised its home price growth forecast downward for the year, basing that adjustment on waning purchase demand because of wider economic uncertainty and rising interest rates.

Construction in certain sectors is grinding to a halt against that backdrop. Marion noted that a sizable portion of recently-built condos has not been absorbed, marking the highest proportion seen since the early 1990s – and the resulting homebuilding slowdown has been stark.

Laberge said just six companies of more than 500 employees currently build residential homes across the country, and the sector is also being left behind in the new digital era. In a recent McKinsey study of the level of digitization across industries, construction came second last, he pointed out – only ahead of hunting and agriculture.

Canada building the wrong home types, says Laberge

It’s also often pointed out that the type of home construction currently being prioritized is missing the mark. Condominium construction, particularly in Toronto and Vancouver, has dominated homebuilding in recent decades – leaving a surplus of smaller condos rather than family-sized homes.

“Canada doesn’t simply have too much or too little housing,” Laberge said. “The reality is that we have a mismatch between the homes people need and the homes the system is producing. What’s small is unaffordable and what’s large is unavailable.

“This is the supply families need and they are seeking desperately, and they cannot find it right now.”

What’s more, the homebuying lull isn’t destined to last forever, and a ramping-up of purchase activity could put even further strain on national housing supply if construction doesn’t gather pace.

“It takes, give or take, six to eight years to deliver a big housing unit, whether it’s condo or rental, in any of the larger centres across Canada. Demand can shift on a dime,” Laberge cautioned.

“Young adults living with parents, people sharing homes longer than they plan, newcomers settling permanently, and families delaying their next move can all come back into the market when confidence returns. And that will return at some point. This is not a one-year story. This is a pent-up demand story that will play out over the next three, four, five years.”

For now, there seems little prospect of homebuilding accelerating to meet the required annual level – particularly with more than a million extra workers in the construction industry needed, according to Marion, to satisfy demand.

Laberge said it makes no sense to ease off on construction even in a quieter market because it will ultimately have a negative effect on the affordability outlook. “We should not close a fire station because it’s raining,” he said. “We should welcome the rain but not sell the truck.”

items.description: New Wahi analysis finds four-bedroom GTA condos up while studio sales nearly vanish
items.content: <p>New Wahi analysis finds four-bedroom GTA condos up while studio sales nearly vanish</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0388_639282832912037174.png" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: New Wahi analysis finds four-bedroom GTA condos up while studio sales nearly vanish
items.body:
The Greater Toronto Area’s condominium market is fracturing along size lines. New research from Wahi, a Toronto-based digital real estate platform and brokerage, finds that buyers who acquired larger units at the outset of the pandemic are still holding gains, while the one-bedroom segment has dropped 14% from Q1 2020 and has recorded flat or negative pricing in every consecutive quarter since Q1 2022.

The analysis compares median sale prices and transaction volumes across condominium types between Q1 2020 and Q1 2026, adding texture to a correction that Canadian mortgage professionals have followed closely.

Wahi’s tracking of GTA days on market through the first half of 2026 showed condominiums averaging 36 days to find a buyer in Q2 2026, roughly three to four times longer than during the market’s 2022 peak. 

Small units feel the weight of investor retreat

The data is most acute at the bottom of the size ladder. In Q1, the median price of a one-bedroom Greater Toronto Area condominium was $480,000, with 1,574 units changing hands. That's down 39% from Q1 2020 and 66% below the peak recorded in Q1 2021.

Studios have fared even worse. Just seven transactions were recorded in the first quarter of 2026, against a high of 230 in Q1 2022.

“In today’s GTA condo market, the end user is the main source of anything resembling demand,” said Ryan McLaughlin, economist at Wahi.

“There simply isn’t much appetite among buyers for smaller units, which have historically been geared primarily towards investors looking to flip them and/or rent them out.”

The broker community has had a front-row seat to the fallout. Christine Xu, founder of Money Broker Canada and a 26-year industry veteran, described the pre-construction investor collapse starkly when speaking at MortgageFest Canada 2026.

“A lot of those people are racing masters — they invest in a whole bunch of pre-construction condos and they are being hit the most. Big shot realtors who bought so many pre-construction condos and now — bankruptcy. We see bankruptcy all over the place,” she said.

On pricing, Xu was equally direct: “The price is almost 50% of the original purchase price. So the original owner walked away, gave the condo back to the builder.”

Stéfane Marion, chief economist at National Bank of Canada, says Ottawa should allow foreign buyers to purchase new-build homes, pointing to unsold condo inventory and the government's goal of making Canada more attractive to investors. https://t.co/hUVWtFthRu — Canadian Mortgage Professional Magazine (@CMPmagazine) October 20, 2026

Larger units offer a buffer — for now

Further up the size spectrum, the picture is more resilient, though still far from comfortable. Two-bedroom condominiums recorded a Q1 2026 median of $630,000, just 2% above Q1 2020 levels.

Three-bedroom units reached $700,000 — a 13% gain — while four-plus-bedroom condos led all categories at $715,000, up 15% over the six-year study period.

Transaction volumes have not been spared regardless of size: two-bedroom sales fell 35% from Q1 2020, three-bedroom activity dropped 43%, and four-plus-bedroom transactions declined 33%.

“Although this is likely not the kind of appreciation condo owners are hoping for, these numbers demonstrate something important about the GTA real estate market in general,” McLaughlin said.

“Even in the harshest environment in decades, buyers who purchase the right type of unit and are able to hold on for the longer term are insulated from the worst effects of a correction.”

“What’s striking is these units have maintained pricing even as sales volumes have collapsed across the board,” he added.

“However, it seems that buyers of larger three- and four-bedroom units have less room for price negotiation.”

For end users — the segment McLaughlin identifies as the market’s only real source of demand — the window may be more open than headlines suggest.

Reaza Ali, national business development manager at Heartwood Financial Group, told MortgageFest Canada 2026, “The market has come into a position now, that those with resources, it’s a fantastic opportunity to jump in... I would focus in on is the affordability piece there, because the price points on these properties are more in line with where they should have been.”

items.title: Amazon-Leased Ajax Facility Listed As Part Of 3-Building Industrial Portfolio
items.description:
Markets speak, and the commercial real estate market in the Greater Toronto Area is indicating that there is a demand for institutional-grade industrial properties, according to yet another new listing for a high-profile industrial property that came online this week.

After a TELUS-leased industrial property and a Tesla-leased industrial property were listed in recent weeks, this time around it is an industrial property leased to Amazon, among others.

The property is an industrial park consisting of three buildings located at 789 Salem Road North, 689 Salem Road North, and 210 Kerrison Drive East in Ajax. The three properties span a total of 107 acres along Salem Road North between Rossland Road East and Kerrison Drive East.

789 Salem Road North spans 58.2 acres, was constructed in 2021, and is home to 1,080,710 sq. ft of space that is 100% leased to tech giant Amazon.

689 Salem Road North spans 9.7 acres, was constructed in 2023, and is home to 181,281 sq. ft of space that is 100% leased to wholesale company All-Special and panel manufacturer SkyRise Prefab Building Solutions.

Lastly, 210 Kerrison Drive East spans 39.1 acres, was constructed in 2022, and is home to 716,548 sq. ft of space that is 100% leased to clothing company H&M.

The properties are owned by CPSP Ajax Nominee Inc. — a joint venture between investment firm Crestpoint Real Estate Investments and pension fund PSP Investments — and belong to the GTA East Industrial Park originally developed by Crestpoint, Broccolini, and Blackwood Partners.

The Listing

Earlier this month, 789 Salem Road North, 689 Salem Road North, and 210 Kerrison Drive East were together listed for sale by Reid Taylor, Lucas Atkins, Matthew Thrift, Connor Molony, Graham Meader, Colin Alves, Luke Dawson, and Edward Plumley of Colliers on an unpriced basis.

  • Address: 789 Salem Road North, 689 Salem Road North, and 210 Kerrison Drive East, Ajax
  • Year Built: 2021 / 2023 / 2022
  • Site Area: 107.0 acres
  • Gross Leasable Area: 1,978,539 sq. ft
  • Current Occupancy Rate: 100%
  • Price: Unpriced
  • Listed By: Colliers (Reid Taylor, Lucas Atkins, Matthew Thrift, Connor Molony, Graham Meader, Colin Alves, Luke Dawson, and Edward Plumley)

According to Colliers, the buildings are equipped with “state-of-the-art” shipping and receiving infrastructure, 40-ft clear heights, and large-format functional warehouse configurations. The properties also include a total of 227 truck-level shipping doors, 363 trailer parking stalls, and 1,160 dedicated vehicle stalls.

The tenancies have a weighted average lease term of 6.8 years, and Colliers says the tenants have made significant capital investments in their spaces. Amazon’s facility was purpose-built for them, H&M’s facility includes an automated conveyor system, and All-Special’s space includes modular cold storage installations.

“At 1.98 million sf, the Portfolio represents approximately 4% of GTA East’s total industrial inventory,” said Colliers in a listing brochure obtained by STOREYS. “Limited near-term power availability in Durham Region makes future development in the immediate area challenging, rendering this scale of product difficult to replicate. The Portfolio is well-positioned to capitalize on sustained demand within Canada’s most critical and supply-constrained industrial market.”

There’s also the location, which is approximately 2 km from Highway 401, provides access to Highway 407 and 412, and is within a 35-minute drive of downtown Toronto. The assets also benefit from the state of the industrial market.

“Greater Toronto is one of North America’s top-performing industrial markets, with a current vacancy rate of 2.2%,” added Colliers. “Demand is supported by a growing consumer base and continued investment in domestic supply chains, while land scarcity and elevated development costs constrain new supply. This offering provides global investors with a valuable long-term land position and immediate scale in one of Canada’s most sought-after industrial markets.”

items.title: GTA High-Rise Sales Sink To A September Record Low
items.description:
Builders in the Greater Toronto Area sold 820 new low-rise homes in September, 17% above the 10-year average for the month. It’s the sixth month in a row low-rise sales have cleared that bar, which covers every month since the HST rebate program launched.

High-rise went the other way. Just 129 new high-rise units sold in September, according to new figures from the Building Industry and Land Development Association (BILD) and Altus Group, BILD’s official source for new home market data. That’s the lowest September on record for the segment, down 40% from September 2025 and 90% below the 10-year average. (BILD’s high-rise category includes units in low-, medium- and high-rise buildings, plus stacked townhouses.)

The low-rise surge isn’t enough to carry the market on its own. Total new home sales came to 949 in September. That’s up significantly from a year ago, and still 52% below the 10-year average of 1,978 units for the month.

Both segments are operating under the same program. BILD and Altus point to its rules around construction start and completion dates as the main obstacle keeping high-rise from taking part the way low-rise has. Altus also names a second problem.

“The high-rise sector remained plagued by undesirable inventory and program constraints centred on unattainable construction timelines,” said Edward Jegg, Research Manager at Altus Group.

High-rise inventory inched up to 12,909 units in September, or roughly 49 months of supply based on average sales over the last 12 months. Low-rise inventory sits at 7,048 homes, or 11 months’ worth.

And within low-rise, buyers are reaching for different product types than they used to.

“In the low-rise market, we have seen a positive response to the HST rebate program with increased sales activity and greater interest in semi-detached homes and townhouses,” said Justin Sherwood, Chief Operating Officer at BILD. “More than half of September’s sales were in semis and townhomes, representing a shift from traditional levels.”

Pricing has moved on that side of the market, too. The benchmark price for a new low-rise home was $1,246,764 in September, down 13.3% over the last 12 months. The high-rise benchmark held at $1,031,574, unchanged from a year ago. Both are gross prices that don’t reflect the HST rebate, so buyers who qualify would see an additional benefit.

Sherwood said the September high-rise numbers show the program rules need to change.

“The high-rise sales performance in September should be a wake-up call that there needs to be further measures and a modification of the program rules to allow the high-rise sector to better participate in the program, which would enable homebuyers in every segment of the housing market to benefit,” he said.

In Simcoe County, the split was starker still: 73 new low-rise homes sold in September at a weighted average price of $998,787, and not a single high-rise unit.

items._ogDesc: National Bank warns Canada’s housing market needs higher immigration and foreign buyers to clear a record inventory of unsold homes and avoid a demographic cliff.
items.body:
Canadian real estate remains out of reach for young adults, but the show must go on. That’s the takeaway from a new housing report from National Bank of Canada. Slow home sales have led to a backlog of developer inventory, but billions in public bailouts are being used to support prices. National Bank urges policymakers to increase their immigration targets and reintroduce foreign buyers to help developers reduce inventory.

Canadian Real Estate In A Slump Despite Billions In Bailouts

The Great Canadian Real Estate Slump isn’t exactly news, but not everyone may be aware of how slow it’s been. Over 1 in 4 (28%) newly completed homes remain unsold, charting new territory for excess supply. “The inventory of completed and unsold housing units across all census metropolitan areas stands at 20,700 units, its highest level since records began in 1990,” warns the bank.

Existing homes aren’t doing much better. Seasonally adjusted sales saw a monthly drop of 2.3% in September, sliding 13% below the 10-year average. While Canadian home prices are now in the biggest correction on record, the almost 5-year slump only rolled back 13 months of price gains. That’s with taxpayer-backed bailouts.

“This demonstrates that the market is so weak that it requires public support,” writes National Bank.

Policymakers aren’t dabbling in support either—they’re fully immersed in the practice. The bank cites Ontario’s $1.3 billion bailout to help investors buy 2,200 unsold Toronto condos. They also cite Ottawa and British Columbia’s $1.45 billion program for roughly the same number of condos. These programs are massive, but even taxpayer-funded bulk buying isn’t enough to clear the backlog.

The bank urges policymakers to drum up more demand. Not from the young adults struggling with shelter costs. They can’t afford to buy a home. They’re calling on Ottawa to look beyond its borders to support prices. Seriously.

Big Six Bank Calls For Higher Immigration To Improve Demand

Canadian real estate prices surged from 2020 and finally peaked in March 2022. That occurred during the pandemic’s population slump, when population growth plummeted to near historic lows. Canada ramped up immigration to unprecedented levels as the slump kicked off. Despite a timing mismatch, reduced immigration is often cited as extending the downturn. The narrative was reinforced by StatCan’s population estimates that revealed a historic contraction. However, that contraction also didn’t happen.

The agency’s recent revisions show the 0.5% y/y decline reported at the start of 2026 was actually 0.5% growth. Ottawa’s plan to reduce non-permanent residents (NPR) to 5% of the population by 2027 is also unlikely. Not only did policymakers delay the target by a year, but NPRs currently represent 6.7% of the population. Canada needs to lose roughly 750,000 NPRs by the end of next year to make those numbers work. Still, the Big Six Bank is concerned.

Reducing NPRs to 5% of the total population will slow total growth to 0.2% in 2027 and 0.1% in 2028, notes the bank. They warn that sticking to the target will mean more downward pressure on housing. “In that context, we believe Ottawa should recalibrate its immigration policy through a targeted and gradual increase in immigration levels,” says National Bank.

Canadians Can’t Afford Homes? Sell Them To Foreign Investors

Canada’s foreign homebuyer restrictions are set to expire in a few months. “The ban on foreign home purchases, which expires on January 1, 2027, should not be extended but rather replaced by a more flexible policy,” explains National Bank.

Whether Canada will renew the moratorium is unclear, but policymakers aren’t fond of the measures. They began to quietly ease foreign buyer restrictions just 86 days after boasting of passing the ban. Canada has since elected Prime Minister Mark Carney, and while he hasn’t addressed the ban directly, the bank notes he recently laid the groundwork for a “controlled increase” in the population.

One of his key fundraisers in BC has been a little more vocal about foreign capital returning to housing. Shortly after PM Carney was elected, Vancouver’s “condo king” said he was working with the PM to drum up foreign capital for rentals.

National Bank sees foreign buyers as one of the only ways developers can sell the homes they built. “We believe it should not be renewed in its current form and that a more flexible model—such as Australia’s, which notably allows foreign buyers to purchase new homes—would help reduce the inventory of unsold housing,” argues the bank.

The bank’s take seems tone-deaf, but the implications are more disturbing. RBC recently found the average first-time buyer plans to buy at 41, 12 years later than current owners did. Separately, they found parents are increasingly helping their adult kids pay bills—a trend most parents attribute to a soaring cost of living rather than poor money management.

Canada’s young adults have been locked out of the housing market. For years they were told that more supply would close the gap, and building more would finally bring prices down. After taxpayers footed the bill to accelerate construction, the narrative abruptly shifted: prices can’t fall further because developers can’t make the math work. Since young adults can’t afford these prices, we suddenly need more temporary residents to support attractive rents that developers can pitch to foreign landlords.

items.body:
How much should governments pay to acquire land?

Under the BC NDP, the province has acquired several private properties for public use, paying what some industry sources describe as an unusual premium.

In fall 2025, the province announced that it had allocated $26 million to the Conseil scolaire francophone de la Colombie-Britannique to acquire 3044 Pratt St., Abbotsford, for a Francophone school. Provincial transaction data records a purchase price from a subsidiary of Abbotsford’s Azure Properties Group of $24.6 million, or $2 million an acre (leaving $1.4 million to cover transaction and closing costs).

On Jan. 29, the province acquired a 40-acre property at 1320 McKenzie Rd., Abbotsford, from a subsidiary of Richmond’s Panatch Group for $27.8 million, or $695,000 an acre. The property was used to grow vegetables, but Infrastructure BC plans to build a new Plant and Animal Health Centre on the site in partnership with the B.C. Ministry of Agriculture and Food.

On March 31, Crown corporation BC Hydro acquired a 21.75-acre parcel of vacant industrial land at 2161 Caribou Drive, Langford, from Vancouver-based developers Strand and Bastion Development Corp. for $52.5 million, or an average of $2.4 million an acre.

Howard Chai, who broke news of the deal at The Realist, noted that the “very specific” real estate needs of public entities often result in them appearing to pay more for sites than what other, less constrained parties might.

In the case of the school site in Abbotsford, industry sources indicate that the price was well above not just the $9.8 million value the BC Assessment assigned it on July 1, 2025, but also previous offers by private developers.

One well-known Vancouver developer who spoke to Western Investor on condition of anonymity, considered acquiring the property after it returned to market in fall 2022. Plans filed with the city at the time called for 130 townhomes on a developable area of seven acres. Pricing guidance stood at $24 million.

However, the site’s challenging topography, marked by steep slopes and fish-bearing streams, left just 3.5 acres suitable for development in the view of the developer. It couldn’t justify a price greater than $10 million.

An accepted offer in the range of $18 million ultimately came through, but during the due diligence process the purchaser reduced the offer to $15.5 million—again, because of site considerations. The deal collapsed.

An industry source familiar with the details—also speaking anonymously—called the price the province paid “crazy” and “a ridiculous amount of money,” especially for a property that would need to be rezoned before a school could be built.

“It’s a massive risk,” the source said, noting that Abbotsford has historically been reluctant to tweak its Official Community Plan to accommodate new uses within established zones.

Similarly, the province paid several times Farm Credit Canada’s reported regional average of $104,600 for agricultural parcels last year to acquire the farmland for the new Plant and Animal Health Centre. With farmland values in B.C. declining over the past 18 months, the province’s premium looks even more egregious.

While the purchase price was “well below” the prices of nearby retail or industrial properties, the site was purchased as actively farmed land within the Agricultural Land Reserve that would require a non-farm use application.

“Why the province paid so dearly for it, relative to what Panatch paid in 2020, is a bit of a mystery,” said Paul Richter, director of market analytics with CoStar. “They did go through the process to get ALC approval to subdivide into two parcels, and for ‘non-farm use’ approvals to permit the [Plant and Animal Health] Centre. This could have added value, for the right buyer. In this case, the only buyer that would have likely stepped up, stepped up. The province.”

The spending practices of other levels of government offer a point of comparison for the province’s land acquisitions.

The Department of National Defence acquired two multi-family properties on Vancouver Island last year to house personnel. A newly built 37-unit property at 244 Island Highway in View Royal traded in early October 2025 for $23.4 million, or an average of $631,622 per door unit—the most expensive multi-family transaction in Greater Victoria last year, according to CBRE Ltd. statistics.

Near CFB Comox, DND bought a 52-unit property at 574 Cumberland Rd., Courtenay, from Simba Investments Ltd. for $19.1 million. The purchase price averaged $367,308 a door—a premium versus the Mid-Island average at mid-year as reported by CBRE of $200,938 per door.

Within the Lower Mainland, the City of Coquitlam paid $3 million—or an average of $16.7 million per acre—in August 2025 for a 0.18-acre medium-density residential development site at 570 Austin Ave., Coquitlam.

The various government transactions, all completed within a few months of one another and involving different asset types, show a willingness to spend well beyond what the private sector would pay.

“It’s definitely a trend,” said the industry source familiar with the history of the Pratt Road site. “With half the developers I have done business with over the years, it’s well known that if they’re moving forward with a property, it’s because they’ve done their due diligence and they know that they can make money doing this. And they do that because they’re responsible for their own private capital and don’t want to lose money.”
